Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 1:

(p-1) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

[Surah al-Kahf]

Its purpose is to describe the Book as upright (qayyim), in that it warns against associating partners with Allah, which is contrary to what the proof (al-dalil) has established. "Glory be to Him" (subhan) [indicates] that He has no trustee besides Him, and there is no god but Him; and it recounts with truth the reports of a people who were favoured in their times, in accordance with what the report in "Glory be to Him" conveyed, namely that He favours whom He wills and does what He wills. The clearest indication of this purpose is the story of the People of the Cave, because their account is the most hidden of the stories within it, even though the cause of their separation from their people was shirk; and their matter, (p-2) after their long sleep, was a call to tawhid and the nullification of shirk. [They begin] "In the name of Allah," to whom none is equal and none is a partner; "the Most Gracious," who established His servants upon the clearest paths through the upright values of the Book; "the Most Merciful," who favoured whom He chose with what is correct.

* *

When that surah was concluded with the command to the Messenger ﷺ to praise [Allah] for being exalted above attributes of deficiency, because he (ﷺ) was the most knowledgeable of creation about this, this surah began with the report that He, glory be to Him, deserves praise for the attributes of perfection, among which is freedom from every deficiency. This alerts [the reader] to the obligation of praising Him through the religion He has legislated in this most judicious manner, by this upright Book, before which the earliest scholars submitted in awe, and which the first and last [generations] were unable to oppose; it is the proof of the greatness, perfection, transcendence and majesty with which that surah was concluded. So He said, instructing His servants in His praise, teaching them how to extol Him, and giving them understanding of the variation of expressions according to the variation of situations: ﴿Praise﴾, that is, the comprehensive ascription of attributes of perfection, "to Allah", that is, the one who deserves it by His essence.

And when He informed [us] that He deserves this by His essence, He informed [us] that He also deserves it for His attributes and His actions, so He said, Exalted is He: ﴿Who﴾. Since the intended purpose is to describe the Book as a whole in terms of its inimitability, without regard to separation and gradual revelation, He expressed it with "sent down" (anzala) rather than "sent down in parts" (nazzala), saying: ﴿has sent down﴾. He turned away from addressing [the Prophet] directly by saying "upon you," as in His saying: "perhaps you would destroy yourself" (fa-la'allaka bakhi'un nafsaka). In this there is a description of [the Prophet] as a servant, and an attribution to Him, glory be to Him, which conveys his honour, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, and alerts to the reason for specifying the sending down upon him, as was mentioned in [Surat al-Baqarah]. So He said, placing it before what was sent down because the purpose is to indicate the truth of his messengership by a means that does not require Quraysh to ask the Jews or anyone else, through His singling him out with what no one else can do: ﴿upon His servant﴾. This also points to the fact that He is the one who took him by night to the presence of His glory, that He might show him of His signs. [He sent down] ﴿the Book﴾, comprehensive of the meanings of the books referred to at the end of the preceding [surah], with what was alluded to of greatness, just as He gave Moses the Torah, commanding justice in judgments, and David the Psalms, guiding to asceticism and goodness, as was alluded to in "Glory be to Him."

Since a comprehensive [book] cannot be free of crookedness, or of the potential for it, unless it comes from the Knower of the unseen, He negated the potential and possibility, indicating that it is from Him, so that crookedness is removed a fortiori. So He said, Exalted is He: ﴿and has not made in it﴾, that is, while the situation is that He has not made for it ("in it" is not said) ﴿any crookedness﴾, that is, any amount of crookedness; rather, it is upright in all its meanings, without any difference at all, guiding to every (p-4) correct thing. For crookedness (ʿiwaj), with a kasra, is the absence of straightness in meanings, and with a fatha, in physical things;

And he follows it with another circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) in his words, Exalted is He: ﴿upright﴾, explicitly stating what is implied, as an emphasis on it, and specifying that it is watchful over (muhayman) what came before it of the scriptures, upright over (muqīm) others. It has already passed, in al-Fatiha and then in al-An'am, from the Imam Sa'd al-Din al-Taftazani al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, that every surah that opens with [praise-4] is for an indication of a blessing from the mothers of blessings, which are existence and sustenance first, and existence and sustenance second. He noted that in al-Fatiha, because it is the Mother of the Book, there is an indication of the four, and in al-An'am an indication of the first existence, which is evident, and in this surah an indication of the first sustenance, since the order of the world and the continuation of the human species occur through the Prophet and the Book. End of quotation. This is supported by the fact that in this surah he mentioned that the affair of those who had seen the People of the Cave from among the people of their time was arranged with the People of the Cave, then with al-Khidr, peace be upon him, many circumstances, then with Dhu al-Qarnayn the affair of all the people of the earth, with what was made easy for him of the means, among which is the barrier that is between us and Gog and Magog, who, when God Exalted brings them out, will cause the corruption of the whole earth. Then in the one that follows it he mentioned, from among the people of His affection and choosing, those who followed them for the order of the world, with what He enabled them to of His obedience, and gave them insight into what they knew of His recognition. He continued thus in most of the surahs until he mentioned the surah in which he indicated the second existence, and followed it with the one in which he indicated the second sustenance. Since the first sustenance requires a respite for reaching the limit of responsibility [and the running of the pen] (p-5) then another respite in which there is the work and preparation for that for which this existence was, from the presentation before the Most Merciful, for recompense by evil or good, and another respite in which the one who precedes among the creatures is held until the arrival at the watering place of death, to await the one who follows, until the reaching of what He, Glorified is He, ordained of terms, for the times of respite, and the standing of all people before the Lord of the worlds. This is the barzakh. And what came before responsibility was similar to non-existence, except in learning the Book, and monotheism, and gathering upon the people of the religion, and fulfilling what they were committed to by covenant [of the rulings], and being trained in it of the lawful and unlawful. It was indicated by what lies between al-Fatiha and al-An'am, which is the surah of the first existence, from the four surahs. It is as if the age of puberty was the first existence from non-existence. And the remainder of life, which is the time of responsibility, was indicated by what lies between al-An'am and this surah, from the surahs in which the downfall of the former ones and the reports of those who passed away are mentioned, as a warning against the likes of their conditions, for whoever weaves in their pattern. It was concluded with praise coupled with monotheism, [as an indication] that it is obligatory to strive that the term be concluded at the highest of the qualities of [the religion]. And the respite of the barzakh was indicated by what lies between this and the surah of the second existence, from the surahs in which the like of that is mentioned in most of it, and it mentions much of [all of it] the death and what follows it of the barzakh, which is for the severing of [the ties] through the gathering of creatures, for the sake of manifestation in the return of greatness, and the eloquent unveiling of the force of the Word, (p-6) and the adornment with judgment by the settling of the two groups in the abode of bliss or the cave of hellfire. And he mentioned much between this and Saba' of the matter of the resurrection, a multitude not found in what passed, until he began some of them with it and built them upon it, like the surahs al-Anbiya', ﴿The reckoning of people has drawn near for them﴾, and al-Hajj, ﴿Indeed, the quake of the Hour is a tremendous thing﴾. And since there was no respite between the resurrection and what follows it for any of that, he followed the surah of the second existence with the surah of the second sustenance, without any separator, barrier, or obstacle. And God knows best.

When he described the Book with what it has of greatness in all of the attributes that passed before it, of wisdom and firm construction, detail and clarification, truth, and bringing out from darkness into light, and gathering every meaning and explanation of every thing, he followed it by mentioning its benefit, putting first what is most important, which is averting harm through warning, because that is its position, as is evident from "Glory be to Him." So He said: ﴿that he may warn﴾, and He restricted it to the first object so that it would encompass everyone for whom acceptance of the warning is valid, even hypothetically, and to indicate that the purpose is the clarification of what is warned of, not the warner. ﴿A severe punishment﴾, being ﴿from Him﴾, meaning the most wondrous of what He has of extraordinary things, through what is in this Book of inimitability, for whoever opposes His command, of the punishment of this world and the Hereafter, like the event of Badr and others, which conveys the entry of Islam upon them (p-7) while they are unwilling, after they had been in strength, and it is from weakness. ﴿And that He give good tidings to the believers﴾, meaning those firmly established in this attribute, ﴿who do righteous deeds﴾, and that is what He commanded, sincerely for Him, and that is from the teeth of the key of faith, ﴿that for them﴾, meaning insofar as they are doers, ﴿is a good reward﴾, and it is the bliss, in the state of their being

Remaining forever therein, without any cessation whatsoever, for "the eternal" (al-abad) is a time that has no end. These two causes together encompass all the meanings of the Book, for it cannot be as such unless it also encompasses all the laws of the religion, the affairs of livelihood, [the affairs of the Hereafter,] and whatever concerns them in doing, forsaking, or believing, along with what follows from these. That is the "upright" (al-qayyim), meaning the one that is straight in itself and that keeps others straight.

Since the tendency in human beings is toward opposing the commands, owing to the deficiencies they were created with, warning was more important, so He repeated it. This is also because the context calls for it, as has passed, mentioning in it some of the omitted related element of the verse before it, as a rebuke to the misguiding Jews for these Arabs and for whoever spoke their saying. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And warn﴾ (p-8). He limited himself here to the first object, so that thought would go off to the second, which He expressed in the earlier passage by ﴿from Him﴾ [Al-Kahf: 2], [in] every direction it could be estimated, so that it would be more terrifying: ﴿those who say, "God has taken a son."﴾ That is, the One possessing unmatched greatness undertook (taka lläf, "undertook") to take a son, as others undertake to take one. They are some of the Jews, the Christians, and the Arabs. Al-Asfahani said: The custom of the Qur'an is that when it mentions a general story, it attaches to it some of its particular details, alerting to the fact that this is one of the greatest particular details of that whole. I have not made the verse one of ihtibak (the technique of omitting from each of two parallel parts what is mentioned in the other), because the meaning is not deficient.

Then he resumed, giving a reason in answer to one who might be asking, as if it were said: "Why were they singled out for this severe threat?" So God, exalted is He, said: ﴿They have no knowledge of it﴾, that is, of the saying, ﴿at all﴾, because it is something that knowledge cannot attach to, since it has no existence and its existence is impossible. Then He established this meaning and confirmed it with His saying: ﴿nor do their fathers﴾, who take pride in their imitation (taqlid) in religion even in this matter, which no sane person would imagine. Even if they had erred in a worldly affair, they would not have followed them in it. This is a warning that it is not permissible for anyone to say about God, exalted is He, what he has no knowledge of, especially in the foundations of religion (usul al-din). Then He magnified the gravity of this matter by His saying: ﴿Grave is the word﴾, that is, this their statement is a "word" (kalimah) of what enormity! He depicted the outrageousness of their boldness in uttering it by His saying: ﴿that comes out of their mouths﴾, that is, it was not enough for them that it passed through their minds and echoed in their breasts, until they pronounced it. Their pronouncing it was repeated, which is indicated by the use of the present tense (al-mudari'). Then He clarified what the speech implied: that just as they have no knowledge of it, no one has any knowledge of it at all, because it has no existence. So God, exalted is He, said: ﴿They say nothing but a lie﴾ [i.e., "in" is "ma"], that is, a statement that has no reality in any respect.

Ibn al-Zubayr said in his Burhan: It is established and well known that the Quraysh sent to the Jews in Medina asking them about the matter of the Messenger of God (may God's blessings and peace be upon him and his family). The Jews answered by telling them to ask him about three things. They said: "If he answers them, he is a prophet; but if he is unable, then the man is a fabricator, so decide your opinion about him." The three were the soul (ruh), the youths who went away in the earliest age, who are the People of the Cave (ahl al-kahf), and a wandering man who reached the easts and wests of the earth. So God sent down to him the answer to what they asked. Part of it is in Surat al-Isra: ﴿They ask you about the soul﴾ [al-Isra: 85], and so on. God, glorified and exalted is He, opened Surat al-Kahf with His praise and the mention of the blessing of the Book, and what He sent down upon the Quraysh and the disbelieving Arabs of might on the day of Badr and in the year of the Conquest, and the good news to the believers of that, and what God, exalted is He, granted them of lasting bliss; and the warning to those who say that God has a son among the Christians, and the greatness of their offence and the abomination of their statement: ﴿They say nothing but a lie﴾ [al-Kahf: 5]; and the consolation of the Prophet of God (may God's blessings and peace be upon him and his family) regarding all of them: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief﴾ [al-Kahf: 6]. The verses were joined with the greatest joining and the finest fitting, up to the mention of what the disbelievers asked about the youths: ﴿Do you think that the People of the Cave and the Inscription were among Our signs a wonder?﴾ [al-Kahf: 9]. Then the verses expanded on their story, clarified their matter, and fully related their account. Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the matter of the one with two horns (Dhu al-Qarnayn), his wandering, and the end of his affair, saying: ﴿They ask you about Dhu al-Qarnayn﴾ [al-Kahf: 83], and so on. The two stories were separated by admonitions and new verses in the most complete connection and the most excellent coherence. Among them is the story of the two men, one of whom had two gardens, the beauty of the two gardens and what lay between them, the disbelief of his companion and his deception. They were from the Children of Israel, and they had a story. These verses have made clear, from it, the deception of one of them by what he possessed and his reliance on the illusion of permanence, and the other's reliance on what is with his Lord and his return to Him, and the end of the matter, after the dialogue that took place in the verses between them, was the removal of what the one deluded imagined to be lasting, and the reversal of that as though it had never been, and nothing remained in his hand except regret; and nothing of his garden remained for him after that great delight except vanishing and nonexistence. This is the state of one who inclines to other than the Owner, and everything except His Face, glorified and exalted is He, is perishing and doomed: ﴿The life of this world is but play and amusement﴾ [Muhammad: 36]; ﴿So flee to God﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 50]. Then he followed that with the parable of the life of this world for whoever takes heed and sees clearly, and he concluded those verses with the story of Musa and al-Khidr, peace be upon them both, to its end. In all of that there is the discipline and rebuke of the Children of Israel, and the reproof of their offence in their hesitation to believe, and the censure of them for their assumption, when issuing their verdict to the disbelievers of Quraysh by asking him, peace be upon him, about the three stories, that they had attained knowledge and singled themselves out for understanding what none other knows. So the answer to Quraysh came in a way that humbles all of them and cuts off their root. In the mention of the story of Musa and al-Khidr there is an indication to them, if they had understood, and a stirring for whoever among them had been predestined to happiness, and an admonition to every person granted success to submit comprehensive knowledge to the One who is the All-Knowing, the All-Aware. After rebuking and reproaching them for what has been indicated, the discourse returned to the rest of their question, so God, exalted is He, said: ﴿They ask you about Dhu al-Qarnayn﴾ [al-Kahf: 83], up to the end of the story. The full exposition of these stories is not our aim, and it has been achieved. Nothing remains except the question of the reason the answer to them was separated and placed in two surahs, although the question is one. This is not within our condition, so we will defer it, by God's power, to its place, if He decrees it. End of quotation. It was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Isra, in the answer, that [regarding this] the soul was joined to them, because it is from the secret of the realm of dominion (malakut), like the Night Journey (al-isra'). It remains that when He, glorified is He, summarized its matter because of the great secret it contains, and they were blamed for their preoccupation with asking and their neglect of what belongs to its world, which is greater than it and greater than everything that has come into existence from that world, namely the spiritual soul (al-ruh al-ma'nawi) by which the whole of existence is made sound, which is the Mighty Qur'an. He magnified its matter by what was mentioned in al-Isra, until the state required, in the perfection of its greatness, that it indicate the reform of existence through it, by what it set free, detailed, and established regarding the matter of the two remaining questions, which are part of the outward dominion, along with what was joined to them of what completed the matter and by which the great worth became clear. It was most perfect in that the things which comprised that should be a surah of its own. And since the matter of the People of the Cave involves preserving the soul in the body in a manner not customary, and then its outpouring, He placed the answer about them first, so that it would be adjacent to the matter of the soul, and He concluded with Dhu al-Qarnayn, because his matter encompasses what he traversed of the earth, and because he made the barrier a sign of the end of the affair of this abode and the conclusion of its matter, and the folding up of what was spread out of it. And God, glorified and exalted is He, knows best.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 6:

When the Prophet (ﷺ) was extremely keen upon their faith, out of compassion for them and out of zeal for the Divine station, which filled his heart with reverence for it, God, glorified is He, consoled him by His words, exalted is He: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief﴾, meaning: as a consequence of this their saying, which is utterly contrary to what you wish for them and which causes their turning away from you, you pity them, you and whoever among your followers sees you in that state, lest you be a killer of "yourself" from the intensity of distress and anguish. He indicated the intensity of their aversion, the swiftness of their departure, and the magnitude of their distancing by His words, exalted is He: ﴿after them﴾, meaning: when they turned away from your call, so they were like those who dismantled their tents and carried off their banners, ﴿if they do not believe﴾.

Having depicted their distance, He depicted the nearness of what he called them to and made its acceptance easy by His words, exalted is He: ﴿in this discourse﴾, meaning: the upright one, whose revelation is renewed in accordance with gradual progression, ﴿out of grief﴾ on your part over that. And "asaf" is the most intense sorrow and anger.

Then he explained the reason for his guidance to turn away from them, without the preaching of good tidings and warning that he is capable of. This is because they do not go beyond His will, glorified is He, and because faith cannot be made to enter their hearts by anyone other than Him. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We﴾, meaning, We do not do that because We ﴿have made﴾, by the majesty We possess, ﴿whatever is upon the earth﴾ of the three kinds of generated beings, which are animals, minerals and plants, ﴿an adornment for it﴾, by making it pleasing to the eyes and by delighting souls with it. Were it not for the harm of harmful animals, such as insects and others, the adornment by them would be apparent. It is evident that if all people obeyed, their harm would go away and their adornment would appear, as it will be in the time of 'Isa (peace be upon him), when they will become toys for children.

When He had informed them of the adornment, He informed them of its reason, so He, exalted is He, said: ﴿that We may test them﴾, meaning, We deal with them in the manner of one who tests, who asks because the matter is hidden from him, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿which of them is best in deed﴾, meaning, in sincerely devoting service to their Lord. Thus what We knew of them becomes manifest in action (p-14), and the proof is established against them according to what they recognize among themselves: that whoever shows agreement with the command regarding what he obtains of the adornment earns the reward, and whoever dares to oppose the command concerning what We have given him of it, acting as though it were only for enjoying its pleasures, deserves punishment. Since the calling of the adornment to the reality of the worldly life, with its idle play and sport, is evident, because it accords with what souls have been [ṭubi‘at] upon of desire, He did not need to draw attention to it more than by the word "adornment."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 8:

Since the call of this world is to renounce it, to turn away from it entirely, and to take it as evidence of the perfection of its Maker's knowledge and of the comprehensiveness of His power to restore creatures as He originated them, along with other matters, which remain hidden because they are concealed from minds by the desires of the souls, He drew attention to it with His words, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed We will make﴾, that is, by the greatness that is Ours, this attribute is established for Us forever, ﴿what is upon it﴾, of all that adornment, nothing of it is difficult for Us, ﴿a barren, barren ground﴾, that is, dust, by destroying that adornment through removing its greenness, so that the barrier against the dust overtaking it is removed; then We impose upon it the suns and the winds, which return it by this to its origin, dust, ﴿bare ground﴾, that is, dry, producing nothing by its nature. And so We do with whoever causes the imposition of affliction upon him from among the animals, whether human or otherwise, equally. Since it is observed that vegetation is restored by the permission of God, exalted is He, by sending down water upon it, to the plant form which is the evidence for the revival of the dead time after time, as long as the earth exists in this form, that mention of this was omitted, concealing this clear proof from the heedless who are occupied with outward appearances, knowing, glorified is He, that it is manifest to people of insight.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 9:

When this was among the wonders [before which all wonders are diminished], and the marvels [before which all marvels submit], even though they have become familiar through repeated recurrence and manifestation before the eyes, and in addition to this the signs that exceed counting and cannot be confined by any limit, such as the creation of the heavens and the earth, the alternation of night and day, and the subjection of the sun, the moon and the stars, and other things, He belittled the sign of the People of the Cave, although it is among the most wondrous of wonders, because it is dwarfed in comparison with all of that. For when a thing is like this, its familiarity increases and it is no longer regarded as wondrous. So He drew attention to this by His saying, Exalted is He, as a continuation of what is implied, meaning: Do you know that this and other things are among the wonders of Our power? ﴿Or do you think﴾, despite the sound intellect and firm judgement you possess, ﴿that the People of the Cave﴾, that is, the wide cave hollowed out in the mountain like a house, ﴿and the Raqim﴾, that is, the village or the mountain, ﴿were﴾ by themselves ﴿among Our signs a wonder﴾, in accordance with what was required by the amazement of the questioners among the disbelievers, from the Jews and the Arabs. The reality is that they, although they are among the wonders, are not a marvel in comparison with the abundance of Our signs, and in comparison with this [plant] wonder which you have turned away from because of your familiarity with it through its frequent recurrence among you. For He, glorified is He, brought forth the plants of the earth in their diverse kinds, varied colours and types, and opposing natures, from a single matter. It stirs with the spring, delights the beholders and pleases the contemplators. Then He halts it, then returns it through dryness and disintegration to the dust, so that it mingles with it until one cannot distinguish it from the rest of the dust. Then He sends water, and it mingles with the dust and gathers it up green and fresh, stirring with growth in its finest state. And so it is every year. This, without doubt, is more wondrous in state than those whose bodies were preserved for a period [from change], then their spirits were returned to them. Indeed, in ancient times some people lived longer than the length of time they remained. This cave, it is said, is [in mountains] in the city of Tarsus, and this is the well-known view. Abu Hayyan said: It is said to be in the land of the Romans, and it is said to be in al-Sham, and it is said to be in al-Andalus. He said: In the region of Ghranata, near a village called Lushah, there is a cave in which there are dead bodies, and with them a dog, a decayed remnant, and most of them have been stripped of flesh, while some of them are still intact, and the past centuries have elapsed, and we have not found anyone who knows their circumstances. Some people claim that they are the People of the Cave. And it is reported from Ibn 'Atiyyah that he said: I entered upon them in the year 504 and saw them in this state. Over them there is a mosque, and near them is a Roman structure called the Raqim, which is in an open wasteland, and at the upper part of the Ghranata area, on the side facing the qiblah, are traces of an ancient city called the city of Daqyus. Abu Hayyan transmitted from his father that while he was in al-Andalus, people used to visit this cave and mention that they make errors in counting them when they count them, and that with them is a dog. He said: As for what I mentioned about the city of Daqyus, which lies to the south of Ghranata, I have passed by it many times, countless times. He said: The view that the People of the Cave are in al-Andalus is more likely. This is the end of the summary. I say: There is scrutiny in this. What favours the well-known view is what al-Baghawi and others transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: We campaigned with Mu'awiyah across the Sea of the Romans, and we passed by the cave in which the People of the Cave are. Mu'awiyah did not reach the lands of al-Andalus. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 10:

When he had belittled their affair in comparison with His sublime signs, His great proofs and His wondrous creations, he summarized their story, which they regarded as a marvel, and which they neglected as a means of insight into the oneness of the One, the Subduer, through that which is the most marvelous marvel and the most striking tidings. Thus He, exalted is He, said: ﴿When they took refuge﴾, meaning they were in this state when they took refuge. But He brought the pronoun forward (into the explicit form, *idh awa*) to show that they were youths, not many in number, and so they had no years through which they could gain from experience and learning what they were guided to of religion and worldly affairs, nor a multitude by which they could be protected from those who harmed them, awake or asleep. Then He said: ﴿the youths﴾, and they are the People of the Cave, about whom they asked. Youths are more receptive to truth and more guided to the path than elders. ﴿To the cave﴾, which was near their town and well known in their city, fleeing with their religion, just as you and the Siddiq (Abu Bakr) took refuge in the cave of Thawr, fleeing with your religion. ﴿Then they said﴾, after settling in it: ﴿Our Lord, grant us﴾. Since existing things, as has passed from al-Harrali in (the commentary on) Al 'Imran, are in three ranks: *hukmiyyat* (ordinances) running according to the laws of customs; *'indiyyat* (what is in His presence), which break the regular patterns; and *ladunniyyat* (what is from His direct presence), which are immersed in extraordinary matters, they asked for the highest of these, so they said: ﴿from Yourself﴾, meaning from the innermost of the affairs that are with You and their most wondrous (aspect). ﴿Mercy﴾, meaning honor by which You honor us, as the merciful one acts toward the one who is shown mercy. ﴿And prepare for us﴾, meaning all of us, do not disappoint any one of us, ﴿from our affair a right course﴾, meaning a way in which You guide us to deliverance in both abodes. Therefore their story, in accordance with what their Lord answered them, became wondrous in its matter, unique in time, spoken of in all lands, at every moment and every time.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 11:

When Allah (subhanahu wa ta'ala) answered them, He expressed that by His saying: ﴿So We struck [a veil]﴾, that is, immediately after this statement and as a consequence of it, ﴿over their ears﴾, that is, We sealed them and held them back from (p-19) hearing. Its original form was: We placed over them a veil of heavy sleep, by which sounds could not rouse them, because whoever is awake, or is sleeping a light sleep while his hearing is sound, hears sounds. ﴿in the cave﴾, that is, the well-known one.

Since the duration of their stay was indefinite because of the polytheism that prevailed among the people of that time, He expressed it with something that indicates indefiniteness, so He said, exalted is He: ﴿years﴾. And since it might be thought that He mentioned years for the sake of exaggeration, due to how far this sleep was from the usual course, He confirmed the matter by saying, substituting for it and making it definite, because the intended meaning of the plural of paucity here is abundance: ﴿a number﴾, that is, many in number. Al-Zajjaj said: Everything that is counted, when a number is mentioned in connection with it and described, its abundance is intended, because if it were small, its quantity would be understood without specifying the count, so it would not need to be counted.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 12:

﴿Then We roused them﴾, i.e., We woke them from that sleep, ﴿that We might know﴾ with knowledge witnessed by others, just as We knew unseen what those who ask were ignorant of, and so they say: ﴿which of the two parties﴾, whether they or those who came upon them from among the people of their time, ﴿has best computed﴾, i.e., reckoned and recorded, ﴿the term﴾, i.e., for the duration of their stay, [for the knowledge of] what (p-20) ﴿they had stayed﴾, i.e., the computation of the period of their stay fell to them [for they were the ones who computed their stay], and they said: "We have stayed a day or part of a day." Then they disclaimed [knowledge of] that [and referred it to its Knower], and to the people of the town. They computed that by striking the coins that were found with them, or by other indicators that guided them to it. However, although what they said may have agreed with the actual reality, or come close to it, it was by way of conjecture and approximation, not certainty and precision, as indicated by the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Say: Allah knows best how long they stayed﴾ [al-Kahf: 26]. When it is known that both parties were ignorant of their affair, [it is known that] Allah is the One specially possessing the knowledge of that. It is then known that He is the One encompassing all attributes of perfection, that He has not taken a son, that He has no partner in dominion, and that He is greater than anything that falls within the imagination.

When the discourse concerned the disagreement that arose about their period, and both parties, along with those who opposed them, were close to one another in ignorance of its enumeration with certainty, and the Jews, who had instructed the Quraysh to ask about their affair in order to create doubt about the religion, did not know their affair in reality, He drew attention to this with His words, as an answer to one who was as if asking, "Which of the two enumerated it?": ﴿We﴾. Or it is said: [And] when Allah, glorified is He, reported about the second question of the Quraysh, which concerns the story of the People of the Cave, giving it some brief summary after the brief answer to the first question, which concerns the Spirit (p-21), the listener was deserving that his soul should yearn for an explanation greater than that, so that his chest would become constricted, fearing that he would be limited to what had come of such reports. So He said, as an answer to one who was as if asking, "I ask for clarification and the explanation of the truth apart from the disagreement of the two parties": We ﴿relate﴾, that is, We inform with information that follows their traces step by step, ﴿to you﴾ in detail, ﴿their account in truth﴾, that is, their great news [and no one other than Us (relates it) except] as a narrative mixed with falsehood, by addition or omission. It is as if it were said: What was their account? So the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, they were youths﴾, that is, young men, ﴿who believed in their Lord﴾, the Beneficent to them, the One who watches over their welfare, who alone created them and provided for them, and guided them by what He bestowed upon them in the original nature (fitrah) of good and beneficial intellects.

When He indicated the beneficence by the name "the Lord," and in His act toward them there was manifest power that is not hidden, He turned to the station of greatness and said, the Exalted, linking to what its implied sense is: so they were guided by their faith: ﴿And We increased them﴾ after they believed ﴿in guidance﴾, by what We cast into their hearts of knowledge, and We expanded their breasts with the gifts that led them to undertake dangers, and to asceticism in the world and devotion to Him.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 14:

﴿And We fortified﴾ with that which We possess of majesty ﴿their hearts﴾, meaning We strengthened them, so that the faculties within them became gathered and undispersed. Thus their state in public display became like their state in private seclusion. ﴿When they stood up﴾ before Allah, Exalted, in the true manner of standing in that [generation] of disbelievers, before their tyrant Daqyanus, ﴿and said﴾, opposing them: ﴿Our Lord﴾, the One who deserves that we single Him out for worship because He alone manages our affairs, ﴿is the Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning their Originator and Sustainer. ﴿We shall never call upon any god besides Him﴾ after the incapacity of everyone other than Him has been established. And by Allah, ﴿we would have uttered then an enormity﴾, meaning if we called upon anything other than Him, that would be a statement of extreme and utter distance from the truth. Then they began to argue that it is an enormity by pointing out that there is no proof for it. It is also possible that when they said this, Satan approached them with the doubt of blind imitation (taqlid), and they answered it, saying: ﴿These﴾ [Al-Kahf: 15], and it is possible that they said this to the king in order to rescue him from the snare of ignorance. The ones indicated by their words ﴿our people﴾ [Al-Kahf: 15] are explained as: even though they were older than us, stronger, and more honored in this world. ﴿They have taken﴾ [Al-Kahf: 15], meaning, opposing the path of reason and the call of the primordial natural disposition (fitrah), ﴿besides Him, gods﴾ [Al-Kahf: 15]; they associated them [with Him] on account of a flimsy doubt with which Satan led them astray;

Then they continued, by way of specification, with what alerts to the fact that from the time they began worshipping [these things] until now they have brought no proof for that. So they said, drawing attention to the corruption of blind imitation (taqlid) in the foundations of the religion, and that there is no convincing argument in it without certainty: ﴿Why do they not bring﴾ i.e., would that they ﴿bring﴾ now.

(p-23) Since they had, by their worship of them, placed them in the station of scholars, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿concerning them﴾, i.e., concerning their worship of them, and they realized what they intended of elevation (istila') by their saying: ﴿with a clear authority﴾, i.e., a compelling proof ﴿manifest﴾, like what we bring, we, concerning the sole divinity of our Worshipped One, with manifest evidences and dazzling demonstrations, for such a matter is not accepted without that. We have gathered all the proofs in demonstrating the oneness of God in deserving worship, by [the fact] that He alone created existence. So, as a consequence of their inability to produce a proof, they are the greatest of the wrongdoers, for fabricating lies against the King of kings and Owner of dominion. Therefore they said: ﴿Who is more unjust than one who fabricates﴾, i.e., deliberately forges, ﴿against God﴾, i.e., the Greatest King, ﴿a lie﴾. So the verse indicates the corruption of blind imitation in matters of divine oneness.

When they had argued for their belief and recognised the folly of those who opposed them, and since they were a people who had no power to resist them, because of their numbers and their own small number, the consequence was their emigration, so that their religion might remain safe for them. Then God the Exalted said, explaining what remained of their affair, linking it to what is implied: *And they said, or some of them who were willing from God's sake, when they had withdrawn from their people in private consultation: "Do not return to your people ever, as long as they remain in what they are upon."* This is if what is meant by their standing [before Daqyanus, and if what is meant by standing] is the rising up with a sincere resolve, then this implied supposition is not needed. ﴿And when﴾, that is, at the time when ﴿you withdrew from them﴾ (p-24), that is, from your people, ﴿and what﴾, that is, and you withdrew from what ﴿they worship, except God﴾, that is, He who possesses the attributes of perfection. This is evidence that they used to associate partners with God. It is also possible that they called submission to His will "unwilling" and their submission to His decrees, in their own estimation, "worship". ﴿So take refuge﴾, that is, because of this withdrawal. This is the evidence for the governing element of *idh* (when, ﴿إذْ﴾, a particle of time whose governing verb is inferred from the context). ﴿to the cave﴾, that is, the cave in the mountain. ﴿Your Lord will spread out﴾, that is, will bring to life and raise up, ﴿for you of His mercy﴾, that is, your Lord who has never ceased to be good to you, ﴿what will suffice you of the important matters of your affairs﴾, ﴿and will make ready for you in your affair﴾, that is, what is of concern to you, ﴿a place of ease﴾ by which you may be comforted. This is pronounced *mirfaqan* with a kasra on the *mim* and a fatha on the *fa* in the reading of the majority of the readers (*qira'at*: the canonical readings), and with a fatha on the *mim* and a kasra on the *fa* for Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir. This certainty is one of the effects of strengthening their hearts with what they knew of His power over everything, and of His protection of whoever seeks refuge in Him, turns to Him, worships Him and relies upon Him. So they did this, and God did for them what they hoped from Him. He provided for them the best of places of ease by causing them to sleep, then He raised them up after the passing of centuries and the lapse of ages, and through them guided that generation in which He raised them up.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 17:**

﴿And you would see﴾, had you seen their cave, ﴿the sun when it rises﴾

Since their condition was hidden, and likewise the sun's movement was hidden from one who does not observe it, (p-25) Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr assimilated the ta' of the reciprocal form (ta' al-tafā'ul), while 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i dropped it. So He said, ﴿inclines﴾, that is, it tilts and turns away. Perhaps the reading of Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub, *tazawwarru* (تَزْوَرُّ), on the pattern of *tahmarru* (تَحْمَرُّ), looks to the state at the point where the inclining is at its maximum. ﴿from their cave﴾, as its light contracts when it rises until it passes the meridian. ﴿to the right﴾, if you are facing the qiblah and turned towards it, or facing the sun. So they are struck by its heat in a measure that protects them from decay, while the cave's roof keeps out the intense heat that would corrupt them during the rest of the day. ﴿And when it sets﴾, that is, it begins to move towards setting, ﴿it cuts across them﴾, that is, it deviates in its course away from them, ﴿to the left﴾, likewise, so that the intense heat does not harm them, and they still receive some of its benefits as at sunrise. Thus their cave remains moist, and there comes to it good air and a suitable breeze that preserves them from decay and corruption. From this it becomes clear that the mouth of the cave faces the Pleiades (*banat na'sh*), and that the mountain in which they are is north of the blessed city of Makkah. It is also possible that the intended meaning is the right and left of one who comes out of the cave, so that this does not necessarily follow. [and—] al-Isfahani said: It was said that the cave's opening was on the northern side, so that when the sun rose it was to the right of the cave, and when it set it was on its left.

The root *q-r-ḍ* (قَرَضَ), which has no meaning other than this structure, revolves around cutting, and necessarily involves turning away from a thing, deviating from it and swerving aside from it. *Qaraḍtu al-shay'* (قَرَضْتُ الشَّيْءَ), with a fatha in the perfect and kasra in the imperfect *aqriḍu* (أقْرِضُهُ), means I cut it with scissors or something else, because when you reach it you come alongside it, and when you cut it you pass beyond it and turn away from it. *Al-qarḍ* (الْقَرْضُ) also means poetry specifically, because no other kind of speech resembles it; it is cut off from speech and inclines away from it through the measure peculiar to it. Have you passed by such-and-such a place? Then you say, *qaraḍtuhu dhāt al-yamīn laylan* (قَرَضْتُهُ ذاتَ اليَمِينِ لَيْلًا), meaning it was on my right. *Al-qarḍ* also means what you give of wealth in order to have it repaid, because you have cut it from your property. *Al-qirḍ* (القِرْضُ), with a kasra, is a dialect form of it, reported from al-Kisa'i. *Al-qarḍ* also means what you have advanced of good or evil, by way of analogy. *Al-taqrīd* (التَّقْرِيضُ) means praise and blame, because it distinguishes speech in it with a clear distinction. They *yataqāradān* (يَتَقارَضانِ) such-and-such, as though each of them is lending to his companion and repaying him for what he lent. *Al-muqāraḍah* (المُقارَضَةُ) means the mudārabah (profit-sharing partnership), because the owner of the capital cuts off part of his wealth, and the worker cuts off a portion of his labour for this capital. *Qaraḍa fulān al-ribāṭ* (قَرَضَ فُلانٌ الرِّباطَ) means he died, (p-27) because when his life is cut off, every bond he had in this world is cut off. *Jā'a fulān wa-qad qaraḍa ribāṭahu* (جاءَ فُلانٌ وقَدْ قَرَضَ رِباطَهُ) means he came exhausted, having come close to death, as though this was applied to him because of its proximity. *Al-muqāraḍah* also means mutual abuse, because it cuts the honour, and what lies between those who abuse one another. *Al-iqtirāḍ* (الِاقْتِراضُ) means backbiting, from this and also from *al-qarḍ*, because whoever backbites is backbitten. *Qarida* (قَرِضَ), with a kasra, means he moved from one thing to another, because by joining the second he cut off the first. *Qaraḍa* also means he died. *Al-maqārid* (المَقارِضُ) means sparse crops, either for removal, in contrast to the abundant, or by comparison with the places of drawing water from a well with little water, since *al-maqārid* are also the places from which the water-drawer needs to *yaqriḍa* (يَقْرِضَ) water, that is, *yamīḥa* (يَمِيحَ), meaning he lowers the bucket into the well and fills it because the water is scarce, since these are places where the water is cut off by raising it from the well. *Al-maqārid* also means large jars, as though because of their size and their cutting off much water, they are the ones that cut off more than the small ones. *Mā 'alayhi qirāḍ* (ما عَلَيْهِ قِراضٌ) means that which deflects the eyes from it, so that it conceals it and the eyes turn away from it, because they cannot penetrate its skin. *Al-qarḍ fi al-sayr* (القَرْضُ في السَّيْرِ) means that you turn aside from a thing in your journey, and when you have turned aside from it, you have *qaraḍtahu*. The verbal noun is *al-qarḍ*, and its origin is cutting. *Ibn Miqraḍ* (ابْنُ مِقْرَضٍ), on the pattern of *minbar*, is a small creature that kills doves, as though it was named for cutting off the life of the doves. *Qaraḍa al-ba'īr jirrahu* (قَرَضَ البَعِيرُ جِرَّتَهُ) means the camel chewed its cud, so it is *qarīḍ* (قَرِيضٌ), because it cuts it by chewing and because it cuts it from its belly by returning it to its palate for chewing.

When He, exalted is He, made clear that He protected them from the heat of the sun, He made clear that He refreshed them with the breath of the air, and gave them gentleness through the spaciousness of the place within the cave's interior. So He said: ﴿And they are in a spacious part of it﴾, that is, in the middle of the cave and its expanse. When He had explained this strange matter and wondrous account, He attached its outcome, so He said, exalted is He: ﴿That﴾, that is, the great thing mentioned, of their guidance, and what they arranged for themselves, and what was arranged for them of this cave facing the good breeze, protected from every harm, and what fulfilled their hope through what none but Him can do ﴿is among the signs of Allah﴾, that is, the Supreme King who encompasses everything in knowledge and power, even though, when compared with this upright Qur'an and other things with which this Community was specially favoured, it is small.

When their being alone in guidance apart from all the people of that generation was a wonder, He attached to it what, if considered, removes its wonder, so He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Whomever Allah guides﴾, even with the easiest guidance, by what the deletion of the yā' in the orthography indicates, *Allāh* (اللَّهُ), that is, [He to whom belongs all the command, by creating guidance in his heart to look at His signs, which cannot be counted, and to benefit from them] *fa-huwa* (فَهُوَ) (p-29) specifically ﴿is the guided one﴾, in any age, so you will not find for him a misleader or seducer. ﴿And whomever He leaves astray﴾, leading astray apparently, by what the explicit mention indicates, [by blinding him to the path of guidance], so it is He, and no other, who is the one who goes astray, ﴿then you will not find for him﴾ at all, besides Him, because Allah, to whom belongs all the command, and with whom there is no command for anyone, has led him astray, ﴿any protecting friend who guides﴾. So you find him seeing the signs with his own eye, hearing them with his ear, and sensing them with all his senses, yet not knowing that they are signs, let alone reflecting upon them and benefiting from them. So the verse is of *al-iḥtibāk* (الاحْتِباكِ, a rhetorical device where two complementary elements are each omitted): He mentioned guidance first as an indication of the omission of misguidance second, and the guide second as an indication of the omission of the misleader first.

When Allah, glory be to Him, drew this attention as consolation to the Prophet (ﷺ) and to steady him, so that he would not wear himself out (in grief), He connected to what preceded the rest of their matter [saying]: ﴿And you would think them awake﴾, because their eyes are open to the air so that it keeps them preserved longer, and because of the abundance of their movements. ﴿While they are asleep. And We turn them﴾ by Our might, while they are in their sleep, turning them many times according to what benefits them, as a sleeper turns, ﴿to the right﴾, i.e., in the direction of the side which is the right side of them, ﴿and to the left﴾, so that the soothing breeze reaches all their bodies and the side of them that lies on the ground is not affected by the long stay. ﴿And their dog stretched out﴾. He used the active participle here because it does not have the sense of the past but narrates a past state, so He said: ﴿his forelegs at the threshold﴾, i.e., at the entrance of the cave and its courtyard, as is the habit of dogs. Mentioning this dog along with the length of the ages (is) with the beauty of this sleep, from the blessing of companionship with the noble.

Since this aroused the desire to see them, He connected to it what restrains from that, with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If you had looked upon them﴾ while they were in that state, ﴿you would have turned from them in flight﴾, i.e., at the moment your gaze fell upon them, ﴿and you would have been filled﴾ in the shortest time and by the easiest matter ﴿with terror from them﴾, because of the awe with which Allah clothed them, and the majesty He placed upon them, and as an arrangement from Him for what He willed concerning them.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on Surah 18, verse 19:**

﴿And thus﴾, that is, Our doing to them this [sleep and awakening] from Our signs, such as sleep and other things, and like what We did to them, ﴿We raised them﴾ by Our majesty ﴿so that they might question one another﴾. He expressed it with the form *iftaʿala* (*yatasāʾalū*, "question one another") to indicate that it was in the utmost clarity. Since what was intended was a questioning about reports that did not exceed them, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿among themselves﴾, that is, about their conditions in their sleep and their waking, so that they would increase in faith, firmness, and certainty through the wondrous matters and strange conditions that were revealed to them. Thus it would be known that there is no knowledge for anyone other than Us, no power for anyone besides Us, that Our power is complete and Our knowledge comprehensive. Let whoever denies Our power to resurrect know this, and let him ask the distant, hateful Jews about His beloved Prophet who came to them with the signs and showed them the clear proofs. If they seek advice from the Jews, let them ask them about what We have related (p-31) of this story. If they acknowledge it, they are all obligated to believe and to turn away from error and transgression. If they do not believe, it is known with certainty that none believes except whom We intend to guide, through the clear signs, like the People of the Cave and others, not through sending down the signs they demand.

Since the context calls for the question "What was their questioning?", it is answered by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿A speaker among them said﴾, asking his brothers: ﴿How long have you remained﴾ asleep in this cave, ﴿a day or part of a day?﴾ This indicates that this speaker sensed the length of their stay from what he saw of their condition, or from other signs. Then, in the same style, He, exalted is He, joined to it His saying: ﴿They said: We have remained a day﴾, and this indicates that this answer was based on conjecture, since He, glorified is He, approved it by His saying, which shows the permissibility of independent reasoning (*ijtihād*) and of speaking on the basis of conjecture that may be mistaken, and that such speech is not called a lie even if it contradicts reality. ﴿Or part of a day﴾, as you suppose when you rise from the graves, ﴾if you remained only a little﴿, for there is no difference between the truthful one and the heretic in ignorance of what Allah, exalted is He, has kept hidden. So it is as if it were said: On what did their affair settle in this matter? It is answered that they referred the matter to Allah by His saying: ﴿They said﴾, that is, one of them said, denying it against themselves, and the rest agreed, by what they had of mutual love for the sake of Allah and mutual accord regarding it. They were in reality brothers of purity (*ikhwān al-ṣafāʾ*) and friends of harmony and loyalty. ﴿Your Lord﴾, who is good to you, ﴿knows best﴾, that is, more than anyone, ﴿how long you have remained. So send﴾. That is, the attribution of knowledge to Allah, exalted is He, results in saying: Leave off delving into this and occupy yourselves with what benefits you, by sending ﴿one of you with this silver of yours﴾, that is, your silver coins, ﴿which you have gathered for such a purpose﴾, ﴿to the city﴾ from which you went out, which is Tarsus, ﴿that he may bring you food, for we are hungry﴾. ﴿Let him look to see who there has the purest﴾, that is, who among its people is most pure and good in ﴿food﴾, ﴿and let him bring you provision from it﴾ so that we may eat. ﴿And let him be discreet﴾ in concealing his matter so that they do not perceive him. ﴿And let him not make anyone aware of you﴾, that is, this one sent from among you in this matter, ﴿of you﴾, if they notice him and seize him. The meaning is: let him not say or do anything that would unintentionally lead to others becoming aware of you, so that he would have caused awareness of the cause that was his. In their story is evidence that a traveler carrying what benefits him is the way of those who trust in God (*al-mutawakkilīn*), not of those who consume and rely on expenditures from the purses of the people, and in it is the validity of agency (*wakāla*). The root *w-r-q*, in all its fifteen forms, has been mentioned earlier in the Surah of Subḥān and elsewhere, that it revolves around gathering. So *al-warq*, with three vowel forms, like *katif* and *jabal*, means the minted dirhams, likened to leaves (*waraq*) in shape and beauty, and through them a person's condition is gathered, and their condition calls for gathering. *Al-warrāq* is one with many dirhams, and it is also one who copies books, and his trade is *al-warrāqa*. "I have never been close to you" (*mā zilt minka mūwāriqan*), that is, near and approaching, as one who competes with you in plucking leaves from a single tree, taking from one side while you take from the other; and *al-mudānāh* is the beginning of gathering. *Al-waraq*, with a vowel on the *r*: the beauty and splendor of the world, because it gathers colors and kinds; and perhaps from it comes *al-wurqa*. In *Mukhtaṣar al-ʿAyn* it is said that it is blackness in dust-coloring.

And "a dove *warqāʾ*", that is, of this kind. In *al-Qāmūs*: *al-awraq* among camels is that which has a color of whiteness tending to blackness. A man saw a ghoul on a *awraq* camel and said: "She has come with Umm al-Rubayq upon Urayq", that is, with a great calamity. He diminished *awraq* like *suwayd* in *aswad*, and the original is *Uwayriq*, whose *waw* was changed to a *hamza*. *Al-awraq* also means ash-colored, and a year "without rain in it", and milk two-thirds of which is water. All of this combines two colors or more. *Al-waraq*, with a vowel on the *r*, is also from books and trees, known, because you can hardly confine one of its leaves to a single color, and because it gathers one leaf to another and gathers the meaning it carries. In *Mukhtaṣar al-ʿAyn*: *al-waraq* is thin leather, from which is the leaf of the *muṣḥaf*. *Al-waraq* is also *al-khabaṭ* (the foliage shaken down for fodder), because when camels were fed it, it was as if it were simply the leaf and nothing else. *Al-waraq* is also the living of every animal, because life is beauty, and by it all matters are gathered, and because the leaf is a sign of the life of a living tree, so it is the use of the name of the indicator for what is indicated. *Al-waraq* is also the blood that spreads round upon the ground, or what falls from a wound, because roundness is the most comprehensive of shapes, and it is a likeness to the leaf of a tree in form. *Al-waraq* is wealth of camels, dirhams, and other things, because the completeness and perfection of human life is by it, just as the perfection of a tree's life is by its leaves, and the livestock graze on leaves. *Al-waraq* is also the good quality and beauty of a people, because it gathers their affairs and gathers others to them. *Al-waraq* of a people is their youths, or their weak young men, a likeness to leaves, because it does not endure, mostly, more than a year, and because it is weak in itself and weak in benefit compared to fruit. *Al-waraqa*, with the *hāʾ*, is both the base and the noble, an opposite, depending on the view at one time to its being beneficial for pasture and indicating life, and at another time to its not being sought for its own sake. A man is *waraq*, and a woman is *waraqa*, both base, that is, having no fruit. From this comes *awraqa al-ṣāʾid* (the hunter became leafy) when he shoots and misses, that is, he did not hit anything except the leaf, meaning he obtained no fruit, but struck a tree that bears no fruit. Likewise *awraqa al-qawm* (the people became leafy): they failed in their need, that is, they returned without fruit. From this also: *awraqū* (they became rich in dirhams), an opposite. This is with regard to the fact that in leaves is the beauty of a tree and its life, and trade makes wealth *muʾriqa*, that is, increasing it. From it is the saying of al-Qazzāz in his *Dīwān*: "This is a man who has dirhams that are *muʾriq*." And *al-muʾriq* is one who has nothing, an opposite. Or it is that sometimes it is for affirmation and becoming, like *aghadda al-baʿīr* (the camel became fat), and sometimes for negation, like *ashkaytuhu* (I made him complain). *Al-wiraq*, with the vowel of *kitāb*, is the time when the leaf comes out of the tree. *Shajara warīqa* and *wariqa* means a tree with many leaves. *Al-wāriqa* is a tree with green, beautiful leaves. *Al-warrāq*, with the vowel of *saḥāb*, is the greenness of the ground from grass, and it has nothing to do with leaves, because that greenness is never free of another color. *Al-riqa*, with the vowel of *ʿidda*, is the first growth of *al-naṣī* and *al-ṣillīyān*, two plants that are the best pastures for camels, because they are a cause of gathering wealth for grazing. *Al-riqa* is also land struck by rain in *al-ṣafariyya* (the early autumn) or in the summer heat, so it grows green, as if that plant is less green than spring plants, and its mixing with other colors is greater than in spring. In *al-qaws* (the bow), *warqa*, with a fatḥa, means a defect. *Al-warqāʾ* is a she-wolf, because leaves that have no fruit attract little desire for their tree, and it is less than the fruit-bearing one, and because the leaf is of mixed color, and mixing in anything is a defect compared to the pure. *Tawarraqat al-nāqa* means the she-camel ate leaves.

*Qāra al-rajul yaqūru*: he walked on the tips of his toes so that the sound of his feet would not be heard, because one who does this is fit to reach what he intends, that by which his affairs are gathered. From it: *qāra al-ṣayd*, he stalked the game, because people of deception are more fit for success. Do you not see that lions are hunted by it, and if they were overcome, their capture would be difficult. *Qāra al-shayʾ*: he cut it from its middle with a round hole, like *qawwarah*, because the garment with this hole gathers what is intended from it, and roundness is the most comprehensive of shapes, as already mentioned. *Al-qūwāra*, like *thumāma*, is what is cut out of a garment or other things, or it is specific to hide, and what you cut from the sides of a thing; and the thing that is cut from its sides is an opposite. This is from naming the place of the thing by its name. *Al-qāra* is the small, hard mountain, detached from the mountains, because of the strong gathering of its parts through hardness, and its gathering in itself through its separation from others, which if it mixed with them would scatter it, and its limit is not known as it is. *Al-qāra* is also a great rock and land with black stones, because it is gathered in itself by being distinguished from other things by those black stones. *Dār qawrāʾ* means a wide house, a likeness to the *qūwāra* of a garment, and because as it widens it becomes more gathered. *Al-qār* is camels or a large herd of them. *Al-iqwirār* is the contraction of the skin and the bending of the spine from emaciation and old age, because each of the contraction and bending is a gathering. *Al-iqwirār* is also leanness, because the lean one has his parts gathered. *Al-iqwirār* is fatness, an opposite, because the fat one has gathered flesh and fat. *Al-iqwirār* is the disappearance of the land's plants, because it thereby becomes *qawrāʾ*, and so it becomes more fit to hold crowds. It is possible that all of *al-iqwirār* is from negation except what is for fatness. *Al-qawr* is new cotton, or what is sown in its year, because it is worn and gathers the body. *Laqītu minhu al-aqwarīn*, with a kasra on the *r*, and *al-aqwarīyāt*, that is, the cutting calamities, a likeness to what is cut from a garment, so it is for negation. *Al-qawar*, with a fatḥa, is the eye, because its place resembles the *qūwāra*. *Al-muqawwar*, like *muʿaẓẓam*, is that smeared with tar, because its parts are gathered by it. *Iqtār* means he needed, that is, became fit to gather. *Tqawwara al-layl* means it passed, that is, it went by, from cutting. *Tqawwarat al-ḥayya* means the serpent coiled, that is, gathered. *Al-qār* is a bitter tree, as if it were that with which ships are smeared. *Hādhā aqyar min hādhā* means this is more bitter than that, because bitterness gathers the uvulae upon tasting. *Al-qāra* is a tribe, because Ibn al-Shaddākh wanted to divide them, so their poet said:

*We called upon Qāra, do not frighten us, so that we would flee like the fleeing of the ostrich.*

So they were named Qāra by this, and they were archers. In the proverb: "Qāra has been treated justly by whoever shot at it."

*Al-raqwa* is the top of the sand-dune's ridge. It is said *raqw*, without a *hāʾ*, as if because it gathers much sand, or because it gathers one who seeks to overlook distant places by climbing upon it to refresh the soul. And Allah is the Granter of success.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 20:

When they forbade their messenger from informing anyone about them, they gave a reason for that, saying: ﴿Indeed, they (i.e., the people of the city) if they gain the upper hand over you, they will stone you﴾, i.e., they will come to know of you and prevail over you, and will kill you in the most vile manner if you hold fast to your religion, ﴿or they will return you﴾ by compulsion (p-39) ﴿to their creed (millah)﴾ if you are gentle with them, ﴿and you will never prosper then﴾, i.e., if you return to it content with it, because even if you are compelled, Satan may lead you, through that, to actual acceptance ﴿ever﴾ [i.e., -]. So they sent one of them, and he looked for the purest food and treated the matter gently. They became suspicious of him, because they did not recognize his silver coin, as it was from the minting of a king they did not know. They pressed him, but he did not inform any of the opponents about them. Rather, he informed the king about them when he saw him agreeing with them in religion, because the prohibition had not been applied to him.

Thus did We [act toward] them: that great matter of fortifying their hearts, concealing their condition, protecting them from the wrongdoers, and preserving their bodies over the passage of time and the succession of events. And just as We did that for them, ﴿We made [people] aware of them﴾, that is, We revealed them to the people of the town in a compelled manner and let them see them. The original sense is that someone who is heedless of a thing, when he stumbles over it, looks at it and recognizes it. Stumbling thus became the cause of his knowing it, and the name of the cause was then applied to the effect. ﴿So that they might know﴾, that is, the people of the town, after some of them had doubted the resurrection of [the bodies], since the belief of the Jews and Christians was that resurrection applies to the soul alone. ﴿That the promise of God﴾, who possesses the attributes of perfection, regarding the resurrection of the soul and body together, ﴿is true﴾ (p. 40). For their rising after sleeping more than three hundred years, together with the breaking of custom in preserving their bodies from decay without eating or drinking, is like the rising of one who has died with his body intact. This is so because sleep in general indicates this, as some of the gnostics said: "Your knowledge of waking after sleep is knowledge of resurrection after death. The barzakh (intermediate state) is one, except that the soul has, during sleep, a connection with the body that does not exist at death. You awaken in the condition in which you slept, and likewise you are raised in the condition in which you died."

Since the truth is something that doubt may sometimes enter, God, exalted, said: ﴿And that﴾, that is, and so that they might know that ﴿the Hour, there is no doubt about it﴾, making clear that it is not a matter of doubt at all, because of the proofs of reason (ʿaql) established for it, which are confirmed in every age by the decisive transmitted evidence (naql). Whoever studies the tafsir titled "al-Zaytun" from this book of mine will attain this experientially. Then he explained that this making-known came to them with beneficial knowledge at a time of conflict and dispute, so He said: ﴿when﴾, that is, so that they might know that, and We made [them] known at the time when ﴿they disputed﴾, that is, the people of the town.

Since dispute generally occurs among outsiders, and this dispute was confined to them, the more important matter was to specify its locus, so He placed it first and said, exalted is He: ﴿among themselves over their affair﴾, that is, over the matter of themselves regarding the resurrection. One says: the spirits will be raised alone, and another says: with their bodies. Or [the dispute was over] the affair of the youths: one says they are righteous people, and others say: we do not know their affair, except that God, exalted, intended to guide us through them. ﴿Then they said﴾, that is, as a consequence of this making-known or the dispute, most of them said: ﴿Build over them﴾, in any case, ﴿a structure﴾ that will protect them, and leave off disputing about them. Then they justified that with their saying: ﴿Their Lord﴾, that is, the One who does good to them by guiding and preserving them and guiding people through them, ﴿knows best about them﴾, whether they are righteous or not, and as for you, you have no way to know that. Then he continued in the manner of an answer to one who seems to have asked: What did they do? So He said: ﴿Those who prevailed over﴾, that is, those who happened to be dominant over ﴿their affair﴾, that is, who came to the fore over it and knew that they were righteous people, ﴿said﴾, they fled with their religion from the unbelievers and the weakness of those who disputed with them. It is also permissible, and this is better, that the pronoun refers to the people of the town or to the dominant ones themselves, indicating that the leaders among them and the people of power were the best of them, [a sign] of God, exalted, having set right through them [the people of] that age. ﴿We will surely take over them﴾, that structure which they agreed upon, ﴿a place of worship﴾. This is evidence that when they prevailed over them and spoke with them, God caused them to die after they knew that they had a long period which no one of that age would live through, and before they had fully investigated their whole matter. And in their story there is encouragement to emigration (hijra).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 22:

When Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the dispute of those whom Allah guided by means of them, He mentioned what follows concerning the overflowing (of talk) from those who taught the Quraysh to ask the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, about the superfluous matters for which they have no way (of knowing), and about which they cannot obtain any proof, any sign of the signs of prophethood. So Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿They will say﴾, that is, the People of the Book and whoever agrees with them in delving into that after their acknowledgment of what I have related to you of their story, by a promise that admits no failing: ﴿They are three, the fourth of them their dog﴾, and they have no knowledge of that. For this reason He left out the waw (and) from it, and its omission indicates that they are not three and the dog is not a fourth. ﴿And they will say﴾, that is, and they will also say: ﴿Five, the sixth of them their dog﴾.

When their saying changed, the saying of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿guessing at the unseen﴾ became very fitting, that is, casting (conjecture) about the unseen matter, hidden from them, of which they have no knowledge in any way. ﴿And they will say﴾, also, as an indication that they have no knowledge of that: ﴿Seven, and the eighth of them their dog﴾. The placing of this after the guessing, although it is (also) a conjecture, indicates that it is the truth. This is supported by the waw that enters upon the clause that is a qualifier of an indefinite noun, just as the waw enters as a circumstantial (clause) after a definite noun, as in ﴿and there is for it a known decree﴾ [al-Hijr: 4]. Its benefit is to confirm the attachment of the qualifier to the qualified, and the indication that the qualified being characterized by the qualifier is a fixed and settled matter. Thus this waw indicates that the people of this saying said it out of firm knowledge and tranquility of soul, and did not guess at random. And in (the Qur'an's) eloquence there is a precious discourse on following the description sometimes with a waw and sometimes without it. So when it became as clear as the sun that they have no knowledge of that, it was as if it was said: What is to be said to them? It was said: ﴿Say: My Lord﴾, that is, the One who favors me by informing me of their affair and other things, ﴿knows best their number﴾, [that is,] which has no addition or deficiency. It was as if it was said: It has been understood from the form "knows best" that among the creatures there are those who know their affair, so it was said: ﴿None knows them except a few﴾, that is, of the creatures, and this supports that they are the people of the prevailing saying, and it is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, who used to say: I am among that few.

﴿So do not﴾, that is, as a consequence of that, say to them with definite assertion, falling under the prohibition against following what you have no knowledge of: do not ﴿argue﴾, that is, do not dispute or debate ﴿concerning them﴾ with anyone who speaks other than what I have informed you of ﴿except with an apparent argument﴾, its evidence, which is what I have revealed to you, and do not do their deed of guessing at the unseen. ﴿And do not seek a ruling﴾, that is, do not ask in the manner of one seeking benefit ﴿concerning them﴾, that is, concerning the People of the Cave, ﴿from any of them﴾, that is, from those who claim knowledge among the Children of Israel or others, ﴿anyone﴾.

Since his refusal to let them consult him (about the matter) required that his resolve be focused entirely on his Lord, glorified is He, it was known that whenever he was asked about something, his soul would turn to acquiring knowledge of it from its source (with Him). Thus, out of his awareness of the all-encompassing knowledge of God, glorified is He, and of His generosity towards him, he might say, "I will inform you of it [tomorrow-]," as happened in these narratives. God taught him what to say concerning every future matter that he resolves upon, by His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And never say of anything﴾, meaning, for the sake of any thing among the things upon which one resolves, whether great or small, ﴿"I will surely do that"﴾, meaning the thing, even if it is important, ﴿tomorrow﴾, meaning in what is yet to come, in any state of affairs.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 24:

﴿Except﴾ a statement accompanied by it, ﴿if Allah wills﴾ regarding that matter in the future, i.e., coupled with the will of the Supreme King, with whom no one has any command, glorifying Allah so that nothing is decided without Him, and acknowledging that there is no power or strength except through Him. Moreover, if that is said without an exception, and the matter is then missed before the action, or an obstacle prevents it, the statement becomes a lie that repels people from the speaker.

Since forgetting is part of human nature, and a person is not held accountable for it, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And remember your Lord﴾, i.e., the One who is good to you by lifting accountability during forgetfulness, ﴿when you forget﴾ the exception, by seeking help from Him, relying upon Him, and entrusting the whole matter to Him, by saying: "If Allah wills," or something similar, whenever you remember.

Al-Tabarani, in his al-Mu'jam al-Awsat, in the biography of Muhammad ibn al-Harith al-Jubayli (with a damma on the jim and a fatha on the ba' that is single-dotted), related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that this (ruling) is specific to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and that none of us may make an exception except by attaching it to the oath. Then (the verse) joins (ﷺ)(p-45) to what the statement implies, which is: "Say, when you forget: Indeed I will do [that] tomorrow, if Allah wills," and similar expressions of conditioning with the will, which indicate that there is no power or strength except through Allah and no will for anyone alongside Him. (It says): ﴿And say: Perhaps my Lord will guide me﴾, i.e., the One who is good to me, ﴿to what is nearer﴾, i.e., closer in greater proximity, ﴿than this﴾, i.e., than what I have resolved to do and forgotten to make the exception in it, so that Allah decreed it and did not hold me accountable; or it escaped me or became difficult for me because I did not couple the resolve to it with the remembrance of Allah, ﴿in right guidance﴾, i.e., in terms of rectitude, by Him enabling me to make the exception in it at the time of resolving upon it, along with it being better in effect and more exalted in origin, so that I will be ever advancing each day through righteous deeds toward the ascending stations of holiness. And "aqrab" is an elative form (af'al tafdil) from qaruba, with a damma on the ra', meaning "to be near to a thing," which is intransitive, not from the kasra-ra' transitive form as in ﴿And do not approach fornication﴾ [al-Isra': 32] and ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan﴾ [al-Isra': 34], etc. And the nearer to right guidance in deducing from the story of the People of the Cave, the narrative of which is about the validity of the Prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ) and similar matters, is to deduce the oneness of the Creator, His power over resurrection, and other matters, from universal principles or from frequently recurring particulars, not from this rare, burdensome particular matter, and similar knowledge of divine realities.

(p-46) When he had finished this instruction in the course of the story, and concluded it with the hope of guidance to the rightly guided, and since knowledge of the length of their stay was more subtle and more hidden than knowledge of their number, he began to complete it, clarifying this hidden matter. He conjoined it to His saying ﴿Your Lord knows best how long you have remained﴾ [al-Kahf: 19], or to "so take refuge in it," whose implied meaning is indicated by their saying ﴿So take refuge in the cave﴾ [al-Kahf: 16], as has passed. That (verse) was concluded with the spreading of mercy and the preparation of a means of support, following His saying, exalted is He, ﴿When the youths took refuge in the cave﴾ [al-Kahf: 10], which was concluded with their saying ﴿and provide for us from our affair a right course﴾ [al-Kahf: 10].
