He said, as an explanation of the general statement ﴿for years, a number﴾ [al-Kahf: 11], confirming His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "God knows best how long they remained"﴾ [al-Kahf: 26]: ﴿And they remained in their cave﴾ in sleep, ﴿three﴾ [i.e., the period of three] ﴿hundreds of years﴾ of solar years, according to the reckoning of the Jews who commanded this question. He expressed it with the word "year" to indicate its censure, because of what occurred in it of the exaltation and tyranny of the people of disbelief, which necessitated the fear of the truthful and their emigration, even though in it there occurred abundance in vegetation and expansion in provision. This indicates that disbelief encompassed the entire period of their sleep.

Since those who directly put the question were the Arabs, He said: ﴿and they added nine﴾ [i.e., of] years of the lunar calendar, when the whole is reckoned by the reckoning of the moon. This is because the difference between the solar and lunar year is ten days and twenty-one hours and a half of an hour, as has been mentioned previously in the discussion of the intercalation (nasi', the practice of postponing sacred months) in (surah) Bara'ah. So when the excess of the lunar years over the three hundred solar years is calculated, taking into account the deficiency of its days from them, it comes to nine years. It seems that the period of their stay, according to the Jews, was less than that or more. (p-47) He then said, by way of answer to one who might say: "If anyone says other than this, what is to be said to him?"

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 26:

﴿Say, "Allah is most knowing of how long they remained."﴾ That is, He to whom belongs complete comprehensiveness [of knowledge]. ﴿Most knowing﴾ [than] you ﴿of how long they remained.﴾ Then he gave the reason for this with His words, exalted is He: ﴿To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth.﴾ That is, to Him alone belongs [knowledge of] the unseen. He knows all of it as it truly is, forgets nothing of the past, nothing of the present escapes Him, and nothing of the future is beyond His power. So there is no doubt concerning what He reports.

Since hearing and sight are the basis of knowledge, and He is described with them in a way that no one else knows in its true reality, he expressed wonder at that with His words, exalted is He: ﴿See Him and hear Him!﴾ Since whoever holds something may have it held by another in his place, either by force or by partnership, He negated that, so the door of knowledge was closed to anyone other than Him except through Him. Thus He said, exalted is He: ﴿They have not, besides Him,﴾ that is, these questioners, and those who guess concerning the unseen about the People of the Cave, ﴿any protector﴾ who could shelter them from Him, or [any who speak] with knowledge other than what He has reported. ﴿And He does not share His judgment with anyone﴾ — that is, Allah does not — so that He would act by something other than His command, or report something not through His means.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 27:

Since it has been established that there is no doubt in His words, "No one can bring anything like it" (cf. 17:88), how much less can anyone bring what contradicts it, given that He alone possesses perfect knowledge and comprehensive power, it is fitting that this is followed by His words, coordinated with ﴿Say, "Allah knows best"﴾ [al-Kahf: 26]: ﴿And recite﴾, i.e., read constantly, ﴿what has been revealed to you﴾. He used the passive form of the verb because the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is certain that the One who revealed it to him is Allah, glorified and exalted be He, ﴿from the Book of your Lord﴾, which has perfected your upbringing through the story of the People of the Cave and other accounts, for those who desire it, without turning to anything else, who follow what is in it, trusting in its promise and its warning, its affirmation and its negation, and for others besides them.

Since what would hold back someone from conveying the message of the One who sent it is the finding of someone who would nullify it, or its being obscured to the sender, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿There is no changer of His words﴾. So there is no doubt in their occurrence, and there is no excuse for falling short in conveying them. Abrogation (naskh) is not "changing" in this sense; rather it is a term (ghayah) for what was [in effect]. ﴿And you will not find﴾, i.e., in any way whatsoever, ﴿besides Him﴾, i.e., even the lowest rank of His lofty station down to the last of the stations, ﴿a refuge (multahadan)﴾, i.e., a shelter and a place of refuge toward which you incline, so that it would protect you from Him if you fall short in that.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 28:**

(p. 49) Since the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was intensely eager for their faith and deeply grieved by their turning away from him, to the point that he nearly destroyed himself out of sorrow over them, and since they would say to him, when they saw a truth they could not refute: "If you were to drive away these poor men and push them far from you, such as ʿAmmar, Suhayb and Bilal, for the smell of their robes offends us, and we find it repugnant to sit with them, then we will sit with you, listen to you, and hope to follow you." He (Allah) said, encouraging him to keep his followers, making him indifferent to others regardless of who they were, and informing him that there is no refuge for anyone who opposes the command of Allah, and that they want nothing but to alter the words of Allah, so He will humiliate them soon and they will find no place of refuge:

﴿And restrain yourself﴾, that is, hold it back and keep it firm in its recitation and in clarifying its meanings, ﴿with those who call upon their Lord﴾, in gratitude for His favor and in acknowledgment of His bounty. He alluded to constancy by means of what indicates the resurrection, the proof for which was the story of the People of the Cave. He said, Exalted is He: ﴿in the morning﴾, that is, the time in which the transition from sleep to wakefulness is like the transition from death to life, ﴿and in the evening﴾, that is, the time in which the transition from wakefulness to sleep is like the transition from life to death. Then He praised them by saying, Exalted is He, giving the reason for their supplication: ﴿seeking His face﴾, that is, by this, and nothing else, seeking neither reward nor fearing punishment, even if they were in the utmost lowliness. He emphasized this by forbidding its opposite, saying, emphasizing the meaning, for the restriction of the verb (qasr al-fiʿl, restriction of an action to its object) and its implicit inclusion of another verb (tadmin, the implied sense of one verb within another):

﴿And let not your eyes pass over them﴾, seeking exaltedness, adornment and transcendence, (p. 50) ﴿beyond them﴾ to others. That is, do not turn away from them, while you ﴿desire the adornment of the worldly life﴾, which we mentioned earlier in this surah, that We adorned the earth with it in order to test them by it. For they, though today they are put back in the eyes of these people, are with the Supreme King placed forward, and they will certainly be, soon, when We raise those of Our servants whom We will from the barrier of ignorance to life, in the highest rank of the people of honor. As for after the true resurrection, there will certainly be for them processions before which approaching is feared, just as the People of the Cave had after their awakening from that sleep, after they had been, in their earlier life, fleeing and hiding in the utmost fear and humiliation. As for if the eyes pass over someone because of what he has neglected of the remembrance and what he has put in its place of gratitude, that is not part of the prohibition at all, because he intended by it only the Hereafter.

When He had pressed His command upon him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, to sit with the Muslims, He forbade him from paying heed to the heedless and emphasized turning away from those who deviate from the path. He, Exalted is He, said:

﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless﴾ by Our majesty, ﴿of Our remembrance﴾ through that adornment. That is, We made it heedless, because the action in it is from Us, not from him.

(p. 51) Since the implied meaning is: "so he became heedless," because Our majesty is not overcome by anything, and nothing occurs except what We will, He conjoined to the verb of responsiveness (fiʿl al-mutawaʿa, the verb expressing the acceptance of an action) His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿and follows his desire﴾, by inclining toward what We lured him with of it, and by disdaining to sit with Our friends whom We honored by protecting them from it. For the remembrance of Allah is the rising-place of lights; when the lights set, darkness accumulates, and then desire comes and turns toward creation. ﴿And his affair has become excessive﴾, that is, exceeding the limit, extravagant in it, going ahead of the truth, so that the truth is cast behind the back, neglected through negligence. Indeed your Lord, glory be to Him, will deliver your followers, despite their weakness, from among them, just as He delivered the companions of the Cave, and will increase you by making them dominant over them, and will repel the tyrants from their hands, for they are turned toward Allah and turned away from all else, while the others are turned toward other than Him and turned away from Him.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 29:

When He encouraged him toward his allies and made him averse to his enemies, as a way of consoling him after He had related the truth of the story of the People of the Cave to those who were seeking to test him, He taught him what to say to them, in a manner that encompasses them, encompasses others, and encompasses the story and other things. Then He said, exalted is He, threatening and warning, as was related from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, and likewise from others: (p-52) ﴿Say﴾, that is, to them and to others: "This which I have brought you of this Arabic revelation, free from crookedness, manifest in its miraculousness, and dazzling in its proofs, is ﴿the truth﴾, existing ﴿from your Lord﴾, the One who is Benevolent [to you] regarding the matter of the People of the Cave [and others], including my patience with the believers and my turning away from those other than them, and other things, not what you have said about their matter. It is also permissible for al-ḥaqq to be the subject of a nominal sentence [i.e., "the truth is from your Lord"]. ﴿So whoever wills﴾, that is, among you and among others, ﴿let him believe﴾ in this which We have related concerning them and concerning others. It is accepted and desired, even if he is poor and of shabby appearance and benefits no one but himself. ﴿And whoever wills﴾ among you and among others, ﴿let him disbelieve﴾. He is deserving of being turned away from and not being paid attention to, even if he is the wealthiest of people and the finest in appearance, and even if his dignity is great because of the severity of his harm and the excess of his injustice. ﴿And We will soothe the hearts of the believers﴾ in both abodes by taking vengeance upon him. The verse indicates that both disbelief and belief are contingent upon the will, by the creation of Allah, exalted is He, because a voluntary act cannot come into being without intention directed toward it. If that intention is by another intention preceding it, it would follow that every intention is preceded by another intention, endlessly, and that is impossible. Therefore those intentions must terminate in an intention that Allah creates in the servant by way of necessity, by which the act becomes obligatory. Thus the human being is compelled in the form of one who chooses. There is therefore no evidence for the Muʿtazila (the Muʿtazilites, a rationalist theological school) in this verse.

When He threatened the listeners with what amounts to this: let each person choose for himself what he will find tomorrow with Allah, exalted is He, He followed this threat with a detailing of what He has prepared for both groups of promise and threat, in an arrangement of lafʿ wa-nashr (a rhetorical device in which items are mentioned in a general way and then explained in order), though not strictly in sequence, in a manner befitting this style, which indicates that He has no equal, by using the plural of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓama, the royal "We"). He said, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have prepared﴾, that is, We have made ready, by what We possess of majesty, a very near preparation, and We have made present, in a manner that is massive, intense, and of complete measure, ﴿for the wrongdoers﴾, that is, for whoever does not believe. But this is a descriptive attribute indicating that the ruling is attached to it. ﴿A Fire﴾, which We have made prepared for them, ﴿whose enclosure will surround them﴾, all of them. ﴿Its enclosure﴾, that is, its wall which encircles it, just as a hazīr (an enclosing fence) encircles a tent, on all sides.

Since the one suffering from heat (al-maḥrūr) has an intense need for water, He said, exalted is He: ﴿And if they call for help﴾ from the heat of the Fire, seeking rain (al-ghayth, which is rainwater) and relief (al-ghawth) by its being brought to them. And He matched their seeking relief with mockery of them, so He said, exalted is He: ﴿they will be relieved with water﴾ that is not like the water of which We previously gave indication, that We revive the earth with it after it has become a barren wilderness (ṣaʿīdan juruz). (p-54) [Rather,] it is ﴿like molten metal﴾ (al-muhl), which is thin pitch, and what has melted of copper or iron, [or oil,] or its dregs, as stated in al-Qamus (the dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī). He compared it to that because of the extreme heat together with its thickness. He clarified the aspect of resemblance by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿it scalds the faces﴾, that is, when it is brought near the mouth, so how about the mouth and the belly! Then He connected to that its censure, so He said, exalted is He: ﴿Wretched is the drink﴾, that is, it is so, for it is black, foul-smelling, thick, and hot. And He joined to it the censure of the Fire prepared [for them], so He said, exalted is He: ﴿and evil is the resting place﴾, that is, a dwelling prepared for reclining. It is as if it were said: "And what is for the one who believed?" So He said, exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 30:

﴿Indeed, those who have believed﴾. And since faith (al-iman) is submission (al-idh'an) to the commands, He followed it with what realizes that, saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and done righteous deeds﴾. Then He magnified their reward by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, We do not waste﴾, meaning, in any way whatsoever, in accordance with what Our greatness requires, ﴿the reward of one who has done well in deed﴾. By placing the apparent noun in place of their pronoun, He indicates that they deserved, by that, the description of doing good (al-ihsan). So it is as if it were said: "What is for them?" He said, detailing what had been stated in summary of their promise:

﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ That is, those of high rank. ﴿For them are Gardens of Eden﴾, meaning dwelling places. It is as if it were asked: "What do they have therein?" So it is said: ﴿Beneath them rivers flow﴾, meaning beneath their dwellings, ﴿the rivers﴾. It is as if it were asked: "Then what?" So it is said: ﴿They will be adorned therein﴾ (p-55). He constructed the verb in the passive voice (*mabni li-l-majhul*) because the intent is the existence of the adornment itself. Because of its preciousness, it is bestowed from the unseen, as a favour from Allah, exalted is He.

Since Allah is greater than everything, and His blessings cannot be counted, and each kind of them is innumerable, Allah, exalted is He, said, indicating partitiveness (*mubaʿʿidan*): ﴿with bracelets﴾, the plural of *asāwir*, which is the plural of *siwār*. This is as the kings of the world, among the tyrannical unbelievers in some regions such as the people of Persia, wear them. Since the aim of this passage is to consider preference and action by choice in an absolute sense, the exhortation to obey Him came with what is [higher than] silver. So He said, also indicating partitiveness: ﴿of gold﴾, meaning gold that is at the utmost of magnificence. Since clothing is the reward of [the deed], and it existed among them, He attributed the verb to them, so He said, exalted is He: ﴿And they will wear garments of green﴾. Then He described them by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿of fine silk﴾, which is what is thin of brocade, ﴿and brocade﴾, which is what is thick of it. Then He resumed the description concerning their state of sitting therein, that it is the sitting of kings who are established in bliss. So He said, exalted is He: ﴿reclining therein﴾, meaning because they are in the utmost comfort, ﴿upon couches﴾, meaning the beds upon which are [the canopies (*al-ḥajal*)]. Then He praised this, so He said, exalted is He: ﴿How excellent a reward!﴾, meaning it would be so even if it had no description other than what you have heard. How then, when it has of the attributes what no one knows its true knowledge except Allah, exalted is He! (p-56) To this He alluded by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And how good a resting place﴾, meaning the whole Garden, and He distinguished it by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a resting place﴾.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 32:

Since the focus of the state of the polytheists is only the immediate (worldly life), and their saying had already preceded, ﴿Or you have a garden of palm trees and grapes﴾ [al-Isra: 91] and the verse, and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, We have made what is on the earth an adornment for it﴾ [al-Kahf: 7] and the verse, and His saying, exalted is He, concerning the poor believers whom they despised, ﴿And do not let your eyes pass beyond them, desiring the adornment of the worldly life﴾ [al-Kahf: 28] and the verse, and it continued until He concluded that the gardens of the believers are great in their beauty in terms of enjoyment, He linked it to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And say, "The truth is from your Lord"﴾ [al-Kahf: 29], with His saying, exalted is He, revealing by means of a parable that what the disbelievers enjoy of immediate comforts is not worthy of being boasted of, because it is subject to decline: ﴿And present to them﴾, that is, to these weak ones and to the arrogant ones who act proudly toward the believers and seek to drive them away because of their weakness and poverty, ﴿an example﴾ of what Allah had given them of the adornment of the worldly life. They relied upon it, leaned toward it, and did not thank the One who gave it to them; rather, it led them to neediness and to arrogance toward the one from whom it was withheld, as an honour for him and a protection of him. ﴿Two men﴾. It is as if it were said: "What is their example?" So it was said: ﴿We made﴾, that is, by what We have of greatness, ﴿for one of them﴾, and he is the one made as an example for them, ﴿two gardens﴾, that is, orchards, which conceal what is in them of trees from whoever enters them, in whatever condition they were, and among the conditions is that one of them be on the plain and the other on the mountain, so that a general blight would be remote from both of them, for blight comes either from cold or from heat. ﴿Of grapes﴾, because it is one of the trees of cold lands and it endures heat. It is both fruit and staple food, through grapes, raisins, vinegar, and other things. ﴿And We surrounded them﴾, that is, We set them down by Our greatness, ﴿with palm trees﴾, because it is [one of the] trees of hot lands and endures cold. It may protect the grapes from some causes of blight. Its fruit is fruit in the form of unripe and ripe dates, and a staple food in the form of dates and vinegar. So the palm is like a crown around the grapes. It is among what landowners (dahaqin) prefer, because it is at the height of beauty and benefit. ﴿And We placed between them﴾, that is, between the lands of the two gardens, ﴿crops﴾, because the spread of blight to everything is remote, since the time and place of the crop are different from the time and place of the fruiting of the earlier trees. That is the mainstay of food. Thus the two gardens were a land combining the best of fruits and the finest of staples, their cultivation continuous and interlaced, with nothing intervening to cut them off or separate them, along with the breadth of their borders, the spaciousness of their sides, and the fineness of their forms and attributes.

Then he increased the description of this man, explaining that he had other things besides these two gardens [and the crops], by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he had fruit﴾, that is, the owner of the two gardens had fruit, meaning abundant fruit-bearing wealth other than what was mentioned earlier, of many kinds, so that he would be able to cultivate (the land) with helpers, equipment, and everything he wanted. ﴿So he said﴾, that is, this disbelieving man said, ﴿to his companion﴾, that is, the Muslim who was made an example of the poor believers, ﴿while he was arguing with him﴾, that is, debating with him in speech, from ḥāra yaḥūru (to return), when he turned back to argue; he did so out of pride over him and to disparage his condition in comparison to himself. The Muslim (p-59) was debating with him through admonition and by denouncing the inclination toward this world: ﴿I am greater than you in wealth﴾, because of what you see of my gardens and fruits, ﴿and mightier in men﴾, that is, people who stand with me in important affairs and rally to me in times of need, because that is necessary with abundance of wealth.

﴿And he entered his garden﴾. He used the singular to denote the category, and to indicate what the speech conveys: that the two gardens, because of their adjacency, are like one garden. It also indicates that he has no garden other than this one, because he has no share in the Hereafter. ﴿And he﴾, i.e., while the situation is [that he is] ﴿a wrongdoer to himself﴾, by relying on his wealth and turning away from his Lord. Then he resumed explaining his wrongdoing with his saying: ﴿He said﴾, because of what had taken hold of him: long hope, intense greed, prolonged heedlessness, and his neglect of considering the outcomes, due to the long respite and abundant blessing. ﴿I do not think that this will ever perish﴾, i.e., will be destroyed with an evident, overwhelming destruction. ﴿This, ever﴾.

Then he increased in rebellion and insolence by restricting his view to the present, so he said: ﴿And I do not think the Hour will ever come to be﴾, taking delight in what he was in, inclining toward it, and relying upon it.

When man is naturally inclined to let hope predominate over him, then when there come to him, from the causes of wealth, a long ease, the attainment of what he hoped for, and being lured on by success in asking, what nurtures him and strengthens and fortifies his roots, fear vanishes, and continues to diminish until it disappears entirely and becomes nothing. So God, Exalted, said, relating about this disbeliever (p-60) what hope had produced in him of security from the evil that fate may bring, swearing: ﴿And if I am returned﴾ [i.e., if someone returns me] ﴿to my Lord﴾, who has been good to me in this world, in abundance, on the supposition of the Hour's occurrence, which he expresses in the supposition with the particle of doubt, ﴿I will surely find better than this﴾, i.e., than this garden. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read it in the dual, referring to the two gardens, ﴿as a destination﴾, i.e., in terms of its place of return, its time and its location, because He gave me that only by my deserving it, and this is a quality of mine that is not separated from me in either of the two abodes. Even if they do not say something like this with the tongues of their speech, the tongues of their states speak it, so it is as if it were said: indeed this man belongs among the cattle, in that he restricted his view to particulars, and did not allow that the wealth might be a lure. What did the other say to him? It is said:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 37:

﴿He said to him, his companion, while he was disputing with him﴾, that is, while that companion was [in the state of] disputing with him, denying [him]: ﴿Have you disbelieved﴾

Since his disbelief was in denying the Resurrection (al-ba'th), he indicated it by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿in the One who created you from dust﴾, by creating your origin, ﴿then from a drop [of semen]﴾, generated from nourishment whose origin is dust, ﴿then fashioned you﴾ after He had brought you into being and developed you through the stages of growth (p-61) ﴿into a man﴾. Yet you denied its return for the one who originated their creation in this manner, rejecting the messengers and belittling the power [of God]. You did not affirm for it in the return what you affirmed for it through your knowledge in the beginning. Then, after categorically denying it, you did not allow it except as a supposition, with the particle of doubt, and this [kind of hedging] is among the pillars of the foundations of religion, which is not satisfied except by certainty. You also attributed to Him vanity, which no rational person would approve, when you made the ultimate purpose of this wondrous creation, in this great development, to be death, which, had it been the ultimate purpose - as you claimed - would have deprived the obedient of reward and the disobedient of punishment.

Since he rebuked his companion, he went on to state his own belief, which contradicts his companion's belief. He said, emphasizing to counter his companion's denial and correcting his disbelief: ﴿But as for me﴾, that is, "but I" (lakinna = lakin ana). Since He, glory be to Him, is nothing more manifest than Him and nothing more hidden than Him, He indicated all of this by using a pronoun before mentioning Him, and said, exalted is He: ﴿He is﴾, that is, the Manifest in the most complete manifestation, so He is not hidden at all. It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to "the One who created you," "Allah" (Allah), that is, the One encompassing the attributes of perfection: ﴿my Lord﴾ alone, from whom no one other than Him has bestowed good upon me in creation or provision. This is my belief regarding the past and the present. (p-62) ﴿And I do not associate anyone with my Lord﴾, who has done good to me, in my worship of Him, ﴿anyone﴾, just as no one has shared with Him in His bounty to me, for all are His creation and His servants. How could a servant be a partner to the Lord! I see wealth and poverty only as coming from Him. As for you, when you relied on your property, you were associating (someone) with Him.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 39:

Since the believers follow the way of the prophets in desiring good, guiding to the path of salvation, and not harboring resentment toward anyone for an evil he has committed or an ignorance he has put forward, he (the believer) spoke to him (his companion) explicitly in teaching, after having hinted at it in what he mentioned about himself of what is incumbent upon him: ﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say﴾, i.e., "And why not at the time when" ﴿you entered your garden, "Whatever Allah wills"﴾, which indicates your entrusting the matter concerning it and other than it to Allah, the Exalted, as the guidance toward it has already been mentioned in the verse ﴿And never say of anything﴾ [al-Kahf: 23], leaving off boasting by it, and bearing in mind that He who gave it to you is able to strip it from you, so that this would lead you to monotheism (tawhid) and the absence of association (shirk). Therefore do not rejoice in it or in anything else that perishes, for rejoicing is only befitting for what is secure from ceasing to be. ﴿Whatever Allah wills﴾, i.e., He to whom belongs the whole command, [it happens], whether it is present, past, or future; and for this reason he left out the answer (the apodosis), not "what another wills" nor "what He, glorified is He, does not will"; [then] he explained that by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿There is no power﴾, i.e., for anyone, over a garden or other than it, ﴿except through Allah﴾ [i.e., the One singled out in perfection, having no partner]. This phrase establishes power for Allah and the disavowal of it from the servant, and draws attention to the fact that no one among creatures has any power except by His decree, so one should not fear anyone else; and it draws attention to the corruption of the view of the philosophers regarding natures, that they act by themselves.

Since he had mentioned what is incumbent upon him in himself, drawing attention to it for his companion, and then what is incumbent upon him [of] explicit guidance in a style affirming that the whole matter belongs to Allah, and that nothing belongs to anyone other than Him, there resulted His saying, the Exalted: ﴿If you see me﴾, i.e., O you who boast of what you have over me! ﴿I am less than you﴾. When he mentioned the separating pronoun (ḍamīr al-faṣl), he mentioned the second object of "see" (tara) and said: ﴿in wealth and offspring﴾, distinguishing the lesser by His saying, i.e., in terms of wealth and offspring, which are the most precious of a person's company.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 40:

When this believer acknowledged his helplessness and neediness, in contrast to the power and pride the unbeliever had displayed, he made the consequence of that follow, as is customary in every conditional, expressing it in the form of an expectation. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Perhaps my Lord﴾, who has been good to me, ﴿will give me﴾ from the treasuries of His provision ﴿something better than your garden﴾, so that He will be good to me with wealth just as He was good to me with poverty accompanied by monotheism (tawhid), which produces happiness. ﴿And will send upon it﴾ (p-64) that is, upon your garden, ﴿a calamity﴾ (husban), that is, bolts (maramin) of thunderbolts and severe hail, ﴿from the heaven﴾.

And since being struck in the morning by a disaster is at its most painful, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then it will become﴾ after having been a delight to the eye through the trees and crops that sway with it, ﴿a barren slippery ground﴾, that is, a land on which one slips because of its smoothness after its vegetation has been uprooted, so that no plant grows in it and no foot can stand firm in it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 41:

﴿Or its water sinks away into the earth, so that you cannot find it﴾ [He described it (ghawran, "sunken") with the verbal noun (maṣdar), because it is more emphatic (abligh)]. ﴿Then you will not be able﴾ you ﴿to seek it﴾ [talaban, "to find/recover it"].

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 42:

Since it was known that this believing man was sincere and that his supplication was answered with approval, it was also known that the implied meaning is: "So his prayer was granted to this believing man," or: "So what he expected came true for him, and the hope of the polytheist was disappointed." Then God joined to this the words ﴿and it was encompassed﴾, meaning: ruin was brought about. [The verb is in the passive form (buniya lil-maf'ul, the form built for the object) -] because the thought of ruin encompassing him arises without regard to any specific agent, and to show how easily it happened. ﴿with its fruit﴾, meaning the fruit of the polytheist man, all of it, so that it was uprooted in destruction, [whatever -] was in the plain of it and whatever was on the mountain, and whatever could endure cold and heat and whatever could not. ﴿So he began to turn over his palms﴾ in regret, and to strike one of them against the other in grief ﴿over what he had spent on it﴾ for its upkeep and growth, ﴿while it lay in ruins﴾, meaning fallen with its roofs collapsed, ﴿upon its trellises﴾, meaning its supports which had been holding it up, so they fell to the ground and it fell down on top of them. ﴿And he said﴾, wishing to reverse what had been lost, out of his bewilderment, the loss of his mind and his astonishment: ﴿Would that I had not associated anyone with my Lord﴾, wishing this because of his reliance upon God without associating reliance on the perishable. This is as his companion had said to him. So he regretted, but regret did not benefit him, regarding what he had neglected in the past for the sake of what he had lost of the worldly life, not out of eagerness for faith in order to attain success in the next life. This was due to the deficiency of his intellect and his fixation on what is perceived and seen through the senses.

﴿And he had no company﴾, meaning a group, neither from his kinsmen in whom he took pride, nor from others, ﴿to help him﴾ against what had befallen him, ﴿apart from God﴾ [i.e., without any aid from] the Supreme King. ﴿Nor was he﴾ himself ﴿one who could defend himself﴾, but rather, in that matter, the affair belongs to God alone.

The poem-like passage above is unrelated; here is the translation of the commentary:

When this parable definitively yields that there is no command except that of God, the One hoped in to grant victory to His allies after their humiliation, to enrich them after their poverty, [and to humble His enemies after their might and arrogance -], and to impoverish them after their wealth and power, and that anything other than Him is merely like an illusion with no reality, He made this explicit in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿There, protection belongs to God, the Truth﴾. [Meaning:] ﴿There﴾, i.e., in such severe hardships, ﴿protection﴾, i.e., victory, according to the reading with a fatḥa (qirā'a, recitation), and authority, according to the reading with a kasra. [The kasra reading is that of Ḥamza and al-Kisā'ī, while the fatḥa is for the others; both have one meaning, namely the verbal noun, as is stated in the al-Qamus (dictionary) -]. ﴿To God﴾ [i.e., -] the One to whom all perfection belongs. ﴿the Truth﴾ [i.e., -] the Established, who does not change or cease at any time, who never neglects for an instant nor sleeps, and to whom no protection belongs in any way. This is according to the reading of the majority, with a kasra [as an attribute -]. In the reading of Abū ʿAmr and al-Kisā'ī it is with a ḍamma, as a resumption (isti'nāf, a new sentence) and cut-off (qaṭʿ) for the sake of brevity, drawing attention to the fact that their turning to Him alone in such crises, and not to anything else, is a decisive proof that He is the Truth and that all else is false, that boasting in a passing worldly possession is the height of ignorance, that believers' poverty does not diminish them and it is not permissible to drive them away on account of it, and that their poverty is about to turn into wealth and their weakness into strength.

Since it is known from this that He takes by the hands of His righteous servants [-] and by the hands of His wicked disobedient ones, He, Exalted, said: ﴿He is best in reward﴾ to whomever He rewards, ﴿and best in outcome﴾, i.e., a great final result. Indeed, the pattern fuʿul, with a ḍamma or two ḍammas, is among the patterns of plurals of multitude (jam' al-kathra, plurals indicating abundance), so it conveys intensification even though it is not a plural. The meaning is [that His reward -] ﴿for His allies is the best reward, and their final end is the best end.﴾

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 45:

When He had completed the parable concerning their own particular worldly life, which had made them haughty, so that it became the cause of their wretchedness while they imagined it to be the very source of their happiness, He struck a parable for the general abode of the world, common to all people, in the brevity of its endurance and the swiftness of its passing away, and that whoever takes pride in it is baser than it. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And strike for them﴾, that is, for these disbelievers who are deceived by the fleeting possession and who boast of abundance of wealth and children and the might of their clan, ﴿the parable of the life of this world﴾, that is, the life whose nature — the nature by which they speak — indicates that its opposite is the Hereafter: in its freshness and its brightness, its captivating of souls by its splendour, its taking hold of desires by its blossoming, its deceiving of those possessed of appetites by its adornment; then its crumbling and the swiftness of its disappearance. It is the thing they were most joyful in and most eager for, time after time, over the passing of days and the recurrence of months, the succession of years and the alternation of ages, such that it calls out against itself, warning against it and making one averse to it, to the intelligent and alert one, the shrewd and discerning, desiring the enduring whose joy does not end and whose bliss and delight remain. And that parable is ﴿like water which We sent down﴾ by Our greatness and Our power, ﴿after the earth had become dry and its vegetation had dried up and disappeared﴾, and by uprooting it as you witness, and extirpating it. He said: ﴿from the sky﴾, as an alert to the far-reaching power in holding it aloft and sending it down at the time of need in a beneficial manner. ﴿So there mingled﴾, that is, there followed and resulted from its sending down that there mingled ﴿with it the vegetation of the earth﴾, that is, the soil in whose belly the plants had been crumbled by the long passage of time, so it gathered with the water, intertwined and thickened. We prepared it with fermentation and a making which none but Us can accomplish, until We brought it out of the earth green, swaying with various colours and differing measures. Then We dried it, ﴿so it became chaff﴾, that is, dry, broken and crumbled, ﴿which the winds scatter﴾, that is, stir up, disperse, and carry away, ﴿until within a short time it becomes as though, by the power of Allah, it had never been. ﴿And Allah is over all things﴾, that is, the One specially characterised by perfection, ﴿Omnipotent﴾ over all of that and other things, in bringing into being, annihilating and restoring, ﴿Capable﴾ from eternity and to eternity. So do not suppose that what you witness of His power is something newly arisen.

When al-Biqa'i had made clear, through these two parables and others, that this world, which brings its people to watering-places and then settles them in valleys of destruction, is swift to vanish and quick to depart, with many troubles and constant distress, through toil and fatigue, fear and weariness, it is like the crop: it comes first in the utmost freshness and delight, its freshness and delight increase little by little, and then it begins to diminish and decline until it ends in annihilation. It therefore deserves to be renounced and not desired, and no intelligent person should take pride in it, let alone boast of it over others. God the Exalted said: ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world﴾ [p. 69]. These two, which are perishable and corruptible, are the most excellent of this abode's goods, and they are "the adornment of the life of this world," which, even if a person lived through all of its days, would be bound to pass away, since what he has of it is headed for extinction. Through turning away from it and disliking it, you know the toil involved in acquiring these two, and the swiftness of their ruin after they are obtained. Yet they may be good if they are used in what pleases God, and they may be evil, so that hope in them is disappointed. Each of them may also be the cause of its owner's destruction, his distress, the badness of his life and his harm. ﴿And the enduring good deeds﴾: these are the pure acts of goodness intended for the sake of God the Exalted, to which He encouraged us by His saying ﴿that He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ [al-Kahf: 7] and what follows it, ﴿is better﴾, that is, than the perishing adornment. Since the most important thing for one who has acquired precious things, for his sufficiency, is someone who will keep them for him until the time of his need, He said: ﴿with your Lord﴾, that is, the Lord of abundant bounties, who knows the outcomes. It is better than wealth and children in both the immediate and the ultimate life ﴿in reward, and better﴾ than all of that ﴿in hope﴾, that is, in terms of what one hopes for in them of reward and what one hopes for in them of expectation, because their reward endures, and their hope is, every hour, in realization, elevation and ascent, whereas the hope placed in wealth and children betrays one at the very moment one most needs them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 47:

When he had mentioned the beginning and alerted to its passing away, and concluded that its purpose is the testing, for elevation through reward or abasement through punishment, and since disgrace and humiliation are the greatest thing that great souls dread, especially when the crowd is large and the matter is severe, how much more when poverty is added to it, and how much more when imprisonment accompanies both, and since the Day of Gathering (yawm al-hashr) is a day on which all creatures are assembled, it is in reality the day of witnessing, and in it greatness appears, so He alone is the one to be feared, He followed the mention of the recompense with His mention of that day, because it is the greatest day in which He manifests Himself. So the Exalted said, conjoining it to ﴿And strike﴾ [al-Kahf: 45]: ﴿And (mention) the Day﴾, meaning: and mention to them the day when ﴿We set the mountains in motion﴾ from the face of the earth by the gusts of power, just as the plants of the earth are moved by the winds after they have become dry stubble. ﴿And you see the mountains, you think them fixed, but they pass away as the clouds pass away﴾ [al-Naml: 88]. ﴿And you see the earth﴾ in its entirety ﴿laid bare﴾, with no cave in it, no cleft, no mountain, no plant, no tree, and no shade. ﴿And﴾ the state is that ﴿We have gathered them﴾, that is, the creatures, by Our greatness, before the setting in motion by that Blast, compelling them to the place of standing, where the hidden things are uncovered, the scandals and the unseen things appear, and the reckoning falls upon them concerning the speck on a date-stone and the thin membrane of a date-stone; and the one who executes it is All-Seeing. So they see and hear the quakes of the mountains at their passing away, and the crashing of the structures and trees in their demolition and the separation of their joints, and their annihilation after their great sight and their dissolution. ﴿So We leave out none﴾, that is, We do not leave behind, by what We possess of greatness, ﴿of them﴾, that is, of the first and the last, ﴿any one﴾, because there is no forgetfulness or incapacity.

[p. 71]

When He, glorified is He, had mentioned their gathering, and it was known that it was for the presentation (al-'ard), He mentioned the manner of that presentation. He said, making the verb passive in the manner of the speech of those who have power, and because what is to be feared is the presentation itself, not who conducts it: ﴿And they will be presented before your Lord﴾, that is, the One who is good to you by elevating your allies and abasing your enemies, ﴿in rows﴾, because the earth is vast and they are being driven toward His abode, for the presentation of the most humble and smallest thing, the most obedient and the most insignificant. It will be said to them, as a reminder of the station of greatness: ﴿Indeed you have come to Us﴾ alive, sound, barefoot, naked, uncircumcised, ﴿just as We created you﴾ with that greatness ﴿the first time﴾, isolated (p-72) from everything you used to accumulate and boast of, submissive and humbled. Then you will say, ﴿This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke the truth﴾ [Yasin: 52]. Then it will be said to you: ﴿Rather, you claimed﴾, that is, you asserted in ignorance of Our greatness, ﴿that We would never appoint for you﴾, that is, that We would not, given the greatness that is Ours, ﴿an appointment﴾, that is, a place and a time in which We would gather you in this gathering and fulfill what We promised you through the tongues of the messengers.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 49:

﴿And the Book will be placed﴾ with the easiest of commands, after the presentation that leads to gathering, by the slightest indication, ﴿the Book﴾ in which the minutiae of deeds and their great matters are recorded in a clear manner, such that nothing of it is hidden from the reader or from anyone else. ﴿Then you will see the criminals﴾ so that your eye may be comforted by their humiliation, a gloating for which there is no good after it, ﴿fearful of what is in it﴾ of the ugly deeds and evil actions and words, that is, fearing constantly, with a great fear, the punishment of the Truth and disgrace before creation. ﴿And they will say﴾, that is, they will renew and repeat their saying: ﴿Woe to us! What is this Book?﴾ as a metaphor that they will have no companion at that time except destruction. ﴿What is this Book﴾, that is, what is its state, being not in the state of books in the world? The writing of the lam of genitive alone is an indication that they had become, from the intensity of terror and the severity of distress, stopping at some books. They explained the state of the Book which terrified them and about which they asked by their saying: ﴿It leaves out nothing﴾, that is, it does not leave behind any treachery, that is, failure to fulfill, (p-73) [and it is from ghadara al-shay', meaning he left it, as if each of the two wants to betray the other, that is, not to fulfill to it, from al-ghadir, a piece of water left by the flood, as if it did not fulfill to them by taking what was with them; likewise al-ghadira for a she-camel left by the herdsman "small"], that is, of our deeds.

When the recording of all the minor sins frightened them, they began with them, and they explicitly mentioned the major sins, though the recording of minor sins implies them, for emphasis, because the situation calls for awe and magnifying the lamentation, and as an indication that what drew them to them was the minor sins, as al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad, may Allah be pleased with him, said. They said: ﴿nor a major one, but it has counted it﴾. Since counting may not necessarily entail the knowledge of the owner of the Book and his requital for it, He negated that by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they will find what they did present﴾ in writing and recompense, without your Lord wronging them [glorified is He] or wronging those who opposed them in it. ﴿And your Lord does not wrong﴾ the One who nurtured you with the character of the Qur'an ﴿anyone﴾ of them, nor of others, in the Book, nor in punishment, nor in reward, but He requites the enemies with what they deserve, as torment for them, and bliss for His friends who opposed them in it, for justice among them. Imam Ahmad narrated in the Musnad from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he travelled to 'Abd Allah ibn Unays, may Allah be pleased with him, a journey of a month, and sought permission to enter upon him. He said: He came out treading on his garment, embraced me, and I embraced him. I said: "A hadith has reached me from you that you heard from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning retaliation, and I feared that you would die before I heard it." He said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say:

'Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will gather the people - or he said: the servants - barefoot, naked, and unmarked.' I said: 'And what is "unmarked"?' [He said]: 'They will have nothing with them. Then He will call to them with a voice that the one far away hears just as the one near hears it: "I am the King, I am the Judge. No one of the people of the Fire should enter the Fire while he has a claim against one of the people of Paradise until I exact it from him, and no one of the people of Paradise should enter Paradise while he has a claim against one of the people of the Fire until I exact it from him [even a slap]."' He said: We said: 'How, when we will come to Allah barefoot, naked, and unmarked?' He said: 'By good deeds and bad deeds.'"

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 50:

When he (Allah) had mentioned the Resurrection and concluded it with His beneficence, through the justice that yields the giving to each person of what he deserves, He followed it, by His bounty, with the origin of creation, which is its proof, in a context that reminds of His guardianship, which necessitates turning toward Him, and of Satan's enmity, which necessitates turning away from him. It explains what they met with arrogance His justice regarding them and regarding their enemy, through their own act, as he (Iblis) did when he showed arrogance toward Adam (peace be upon him) on account of his origin. So they showed arrogance toward the poor among the believers on account of their lineage, their wealth and their tribes, and their deed was the same as his deed. Thus he became their exemplar, though he is their enemy, and they did not follow the best of His creation, who is their guardian and who knows Him best of all people. Thus He, exalted is He, said, joining it by ﴿and strike﴾ [al-Kahf: 45] ﴿and when﴾, that is, and mention to them when ﴿We said﴾ by the greatness that is Ours ﴿to the angels﴾, who are the most obedient of things to Our commands, and Iblis was among them. Ibn Kathir said: That is because he had imitated the acts of the angels, resembled them, worshipped and practised asceticism, and for this reason he entered into their address and disobeyed by opposing it. ﴿Prostrate to Adam﴾, your father, as a favour from Us upon him, for which you owe Us gratitude. ﴿So they prostrated﴾, all of them, ﴿except Iblis﴾. It is as if it were said: what is wrong with him, that he did not prostrate? It was said: ﴿he was﴾, that is, because he was ﴿of the jinn﴾, those created from fire. Perhaps, since fire is luminous, though its luminosity is mixed with turbidity and burning, he was counted among the angels because the two elements are joined in general light, together with the worship that had come to dominate him. Muslim related in his Sahih, from Aisha (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The angels were created from light, the jinn were created from a smokeless fire - and in another narration: Iblis - and Adam was created from what has been described to you." And in Ibn Abi al-Dunya's Maka'id al-Shaytan, from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), that the jinn were a tribe of the angels.

Since most of the jinn are corrupt, returning to the origin which is (p-76) the burning fire that harms whatever touches it and corrupts it, He attributed his transgression as being outside of them, and so He said: ﴿So he transgressed﴾, that is, he went out. It is said: the mouse transgressed from its hole when it came out for mischief and corruption.

﴿from the command of his Lord﴾, that is, his master and owner who did good to him by originating him and by other favours, concerning your father, when he showed arrogance toward him, so his Lord expelled him on your account. So do not follow his example in boasting and arrogance toward the weak, for whoever's sin is pride, his righteousness is not hoped for, and whoever's sin is disobedience, his righteousness is hoped for. Then He based upon this what is worthy of denunciation, and He said, in the mode of address because it is more indicative of the extremity of anger and more painful in rebuke, and in the first person plural because it is more explicit about the intended tawhid: ﴿Will you then take him﴾, that is, will he transgress by your belittling him so that he is expelled for your sake, and that would be a cause for you to take him ﴿and his offspring﴾ as partners to Me ﴿as allies﴾ for you ﴿instead of Me﴾, that is, taking that begins from other than Me or from a lower rank than My rank, so that the taking encompasses independence and partnership. Had the meaning been "instead of My taking", it would have indicated independence only; and if the taking had originated from Him, by His being the one who commands it, it would not be forbidden. And I am your guardian, who favours you (p-77) ﴿while they are an enemy to you﴾. Since the form faʿūl is for emphasis, especially as it resembles exaggeration in such expressions, it dispensed with the plural form, and so He said: ﴿enemy﴾, indicating that they are, in their intense hostility, of one heart. Since this act is the most worthy of blame, He connected to it His saying: ﴿Evil﴾, and the original would have been "for you," but He made this pronoun explicit in order to attach the act to the description and to generalize, so He said: ﴿for the wrongdoers as a substitute﴾, when they exchange for one who has no share of the command one who has all of the command and is their guardian, while they have an enemy.

When the partner does not single out the performance of a great matter in which he shares without his partner's knowledge, he said, giving the reason for censuring this wrongdoing with what indicates their lowliness from this rank, shifting in the mode of speech to abstraction from the appearance of greatness, lest a captious person among the associators find fault, just as he shifted in ﴿besides Me﴾ [al-Kahf: 50] for the same reason: ﴿I did not make them witness﴾, that is Iblis and his offspring, ﴿the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾, any kind of making witness; ﴿nor the creation of themselves﴾, indicating that they are created, and that it is not valid in the mind of any rational person for a created being to be a partner to its Creator at all; ﴿nor was I﴾, that is, eternally and forever, ﴿taking them﴾. The original form would be this, but he brought it out as guidance that one who misleads should not be sought for help, because along with his not benefiting, he harms. So the Exalted said: ﴿taking those who mislead as helpers﴾, indicating that one should not grieve over the loss of anyone's submission to Islam, for whoever Allah knows to have good in him, He makes him hear, and whoever He does not make hear is a misguider, not fit to support the religion.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 52 (part 1 of 2):

When he had established the decisive proof of how far their rank was from the station into which they had placed them through polytheism, he followed it with an explanation that, despite their being of no benefit to them in this world, they would abandon them in the Hereafter when they most need them, disappointing their assumption that they would bring them near to God (zulfa). So He, exalted is He, said, joining it by conjunction to ﴿And when We said﴾ [18:50], shifting to the third-person form (maqam al-ghayba), indicating their distance from His exalted presence (hadrat al-shamma') and His transcendence above what might be imagined from His saying ﴿And they will be presented before your Lord in rows: "You have come to Us just as We created you the first time"﴾ [18:48], in the veil of majesty and greatness. Hamza, in his recitation with the nun (ḥamza is one of the readers, and "recitation" here refers to the variant readings, qira'at), followed the style of the first person plural, which was used there, together with an added sense of grandeur: ﴿And [mention] the Day when He will say﴾, that is, mention the Day when God will say to them, mocking them: ﴿"Call My partners, whom you claimed"﴾ and He clarified that the idafa (possessive construction) is not in its literal sense, but is a rebuke to them. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿"whom you claimed"﴾ to be partners, ﴿so they will call upon them﴾, persisting in ignorance and error, ﴿but they will not respond to them﴾, that is, they will not seek to answer them, turning away from them in contempt and occupied with themselves, let alone helping them.

Since they were at the utmost in regarding it as unlikely that they would be separated from what they worshipped, He said, in the position of grandeur: ﴿And We will place between them﴾, that is, between the polytheists and the partners, ﴿a barrier (mawbiq)﴾ (p-79) that is, a destruction or a place of destruction, a separating, intervening barrier between them, a powerful, firm, enduring, guarded destruction from which none of them will escape. I have explained it thus because it is like His saying ﴿And We separated them﴾ [10:28], that is, by hearts, meaning that We turned what had been a bond between them into enmity; and like His saying ﴿Our Lord, these misled us, so give them a double punishment of the Fire﴾ [7:38], and ﴿These are our partners whom we used to call upon besides You﴾ [16:86], and the like, because the meaning of all of this is that He changes the love and connection that existed between them in the world into hatred and severance, as He said: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection, some of you will disbelieve in others and curse one another﴾ [29:25], and that each party seeks destruction for the other, which requires that all of them gather in it. This is what the verses of the Book guide to regarding the meaning. Ibn Kathir related from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he said: "It is a deep valley by which, on the Day of Resurrection, the people of guidance and the people of misguidance will be separated." Al-Hasan al-Basri said: "It is enmity."

As for deriving it from the wording: the root w-b-q (with its yā'ī and wāwī forms, hamzated and unhamzated) has eleven combinations. One is yā'ī: baqiya; six are wāwī: qabā, qawaba, baqawa, bawaqa, waqaba, and baqa; and four are hamzated: qaba'a, qa'iba, ba'aqa, and aba'qa. All of them revolve around gathering, and especially the arrangement waqaba, which revolves around an intervening barrier between two things, and entails strength, firmness, preservation, and destruction, whether in potential or in actuality. For whoever is cut off from something has been destroyed by the loss of that thing in actuality if the barrier is death, and in potentiality if it is something else. It is said: qabā al-shay': he gathered it with his fingers; qabā al-bināʾ: he raised the building; qabā al-zaʿfarān: he picked the saffron; al-qabā (with short vowel): a plant, because it is the cause of gathering for grazing and benefiting from it, and it is also gathered; al-qabā: the bending of a thing, because it is closer to the gathering of some of its parts with others; al-qabwa: the joining of what is between the two lips; from it comes al-qabāʾ (a garment), and qabbāhu taqbiyatan: he gathered him, that is, he gathered him until he was as if in a place of being gathered; qabbā ʿalayhi taqbiyatan: he attacked him in his affair, because it was as if he had put him in a pit; and al-thawb: he made a qabāʾ from it; taqabbā al-qabāʾ: he wore it; and Zayd: he came to him from behind, because whoever wants to throw someone into a pit does so by deceiving him; taqabbā al-shay': it became like a dome; imraʾa qābiya: a woman who picks and gathers saffron; al-qābiyāʾ: the base person, because it is an intensive form, indicating abundant gathering and the greed that are inherent in baseness; banū qābiyāʾ: those who gather to drink wine, because it is a state that reveals the baseness of the base; Qubāʾ (with a damma, may be masculine, and may be shortened): a place near the Noble Madinah, and a place between Makkah and Basra; inqabā: he hid himself; qabā qawsayn and qibāʾ qawsayn (like kisāʾ): he bent two bows; al-muqabbī: one who has much fat, as if he gathered for himself from it, through ease, what became like a building; al-qabāyah: the desert, because it gathers what is in it as the dome, the qabāʾ, and the waqba gather what is in them.

From its hamzated forms: qaba'a al-ṭaʿām (like jamaʿa): he ate it; from drink: he became full; al-qaba'a: a grass that is grazed, because livestock gather to graze on it.

From the wāwī forms: qāba al-arḍ yaqūbuhā and qawwabahā: he dug in it a shape resembling a hollow circle, because the circle is the most inclusive of what is other than it and of itself, since it has no separating angles. Qawwabtu al-arḍ: I dug up the land. Al-qūba: what appears on the body and emerges from it, because it is generally in the shape of a circle. Tqawwaba jiluduhu: the mange left him, and the hair fell out from him, either from removal, or because its marks are like circles. Qawwaba al-shay': he uprooted it from its root, because its trace, when it is uprooted, is a round pit. Tqawwaba huwa: he was uprooted. Al-qāʾiba and al-qāba: the egg, because by its roundness it resembles that pit. Al-qawb (with fatha): (p-82) the bird's splitting of its egg; and (with damma): the chick, because it comes from them. In the proverb: "She escaped the qā'iba from the qub," said of one who has separated from his companion. Al-qūbī: one addicted to eating the chicks, that is, the young birds. Al-qawab (like ṣurad): the shells of eggs. Taqawwabat al-bayḍa: the egg became hollow, that is, dug out. Umm qawb: the calamity, because it gathers what it strikes, as if a pit had swallowed it. Qāba: he drew near, because nearness is the beginning of gathering. Qāba: he fled, that is, he was stripped of nearness, an opposite meaning. Qāba: he split, that is, he broke the gathering, so it is also from removal. Qāb qaws and qībuh: its measure, because the bow is like half a circle of that pit. Al-qāb: what is between the grip and the string, because it is part of that. Each bow has two qābs. Al-aswad al-mutaqawwib: the black snake that has shed its skin, because that skin is round and resembles a hollow. Iqtāba al-shay': he chose it, that is, gathered it towards himself. Rajul malīʾ qūbah (like humazah): one who is firmly settled at home, residing, from firmness, which is a necessary consequence of gathering. Qawiba min al-ghubār: he became dusty with dust, either because whoever digs such a pit becomes dusty, or because dust accumulated on him until it covered him, so that it became for him like that pit.

From its hamzated forms: qa'iba al-ṭaʿām (like manaʿa): he ate it; and water: he drank it, like qa'iba (like fariḥa), or he drank all that was in the vessel. Qa'iba from the drink: he became full; and he is miq'ab (like minbar): one who drinks much water. A vessel qawʾab: one that takes much water. So it is, as you see, a gathering specific to eating and drinking, or it means he gathered it into the hollow of his belly.

From the wāwī forms: baqāhu bi-ʿaynihi: he looked at him, which is from the preservation necessary for gathering. Ub-qu-hu baqwataka mālaka and baqāwataka mālaka, that is, preserve it as you preserve your property. Baqawtuhu: I waited for him. This returns to firmness and watchfulness, which return to preservation, and preservation entails firmness.

From the yā'ī forms: baqiya al-shay' baqā'an: it remained and lasted, the opposite of perishing (fanā). The noun is al-baqwā (like daʿwā), and it may be pronounced al-buqwā, and al-buqyā (with damma), and al-baqiyya. The feminine al-bāqiya may be placed in the position of the verbal noun.

From its wāwī forms: al-būqa: the gathering, and the single downpour of heavy rain, or the severe one, tanbāq, that it descended from a hollow because of its intensity. Al-bawāʾiq: the habits, because they gather whoever is accustomed to them. Al-bawāʾiq: evils, because they are destructive, so it is as if they cause one to fall into destruction. Al-būq (with damma): a beak-like thing that the miller blows into, or what is blown into and played generally, because by its hollowness it resembles a hollow. Al-būq also: falsehood and lies, because its sound is most like that. Al-mubawwaq (like muʿazzam): false speech. Al-būq (with fatha): one who does not keep a secret, because when the būq is blown it makes a sound. Al-būqa: a thin tree, because by its thinness destruction quickly reaches it, like one who has fallen into a hollow. (p-84) Al-bā'iqa: the calamity, as if it pushes whoever it reaches into the hollow. Inbāqat ʿalayhi bāʾiqa: it burst open. Bāqa: he came with evil and quarrels, from this. Likewise bāqa, that is, he transgressed against a person. Inbāqa bihi: he wronged him. Al-bā'iqa al-qawm: it struck them, like inbāqat ʿalayhim, that is, it came out of a hollow because of its intensity. Al-bāqa: a bundle of herbs, because they are gathered. Bāqa bika: he appeared to you from absence, as if he had been in a pit and came out. From this: Bāqa Fulān: he attacked a people without their permission. Bāqa al-qawm: he robbed them. Bāqa bihi: he encompassed him, that is, surrounded him as a hollow surrounds. Bāqa al-qawmu ʿalayhi: they gathered and killed him unjustly. Bāqa al-māl: the property was corrupted and perished, like the state of one who has fallen into a pit. From this: matāʿ bā'iq: goods with no value. Tabawwaqa fī al-māshiya: death fell upon the livestock and spread. Al-khāq bāq: the sound of the vagina at intercourse, because it is from gathering, and because the vagina is a hollow. From its hamzated forms: bāʾatha-hum al-dāhiya bāʾūqan: the calamity struck them. Inbāʾaqa ʿalayhimu al-dahr: fate attacked them with calamity.

From the wāwī forms: al-waqba: a great opening with shade in it. Al-waqb and al-waqba: a depression in rock where water collects; and it is said: it is like a well in rock, a man's height or two, where rainwater stagnates. Every hollow in the body is waqb, like the hollow of the eye and shoulder. The two waqbān of a horse: two depressions above its eyes. Waqb al-maḥāla (the pulley): the hole into which the axle enters. Waqbat al-duhn: its soaking. Likewise waqbat al-thariyd. Waqaba al-shay': it entered the hollow. Awqaba al-shay': he caused it to enter. Rakiyya waqbāʾ: a well whose water is deep. Imraʾa mīqāb: a woman of wide vagina. The sons of al-Mīqāb: they are ascribed to their mother, meaning to insult them by this. Al-Mīqāb: a man who drinks much water, and a foolish woman. The journey of al-Mīqāb: to continue traveling a full day and night, as if that is the journey of a fool who does not spare his mount. Waqaba al-qamar wuqūban: the moon entered the shadow that eclipses it, as if a pit had swallowed it. Waqabat al-shams wuqūban: the sun set likewise. It is said: everything that sets has waqaba. Waqaba al-ẓalām: darkness came, that is, it became like a hollow, swallowing light, or swallowing all in existence so that it veiled it from light. A man waqb: a fool, as if he were a vessel for everything he hears, with no capacity to distinguish his good from his bad. The feminine is waqba. Tha'lab said: al-waqb is the lowly, that is, because he follows his own desire, so he becomes like a hollow that rejects nothing thrown into it. Waqaba al-faras waqban: the sound of the horse's sheath, that is, the sheath of its member. It is said: the sound of the horse's testicles shaking in its sheath, because the sheath of its testicles is like a hollow, so this is the naming of a place for what is in it. Al-qibba (like ʿidda): the rennet of a sheep when it is large; Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: this does not occur except in sheep, because the resemblance of the rennet to a hollow is clear. Al-waqbāʾ: a place extended and shortened. Al-waqbā: water belonging to Banu Mazin, because it gathers them as the hollow gathers what is in it. Al-awqāb: household goods like the cooking pot, the millstones, and the poles, because the house is to them like a hollow in gathering them, or because they gather the family of whoever is in it. Al-mīqab: tranquility. Awqaba al-qawm: they were hungry, that is, they prepared to put food into the hollow of the belly. A dhakar awqab: one who penetrates much in the vulvas, because they are like the awqāb, the hollows. Al-waqb: approach and arrival, and it is the cause of gathering.

Waqaba (like waʿada, wajila, and wariha) waqūban and mawqiban: he perished, that is, he fell into a hollow, that is, a pit, like istawqaba. And like majlis: the place of destruction and imprisonment, and a valley in Hell; and every thing that comes between two things, because the hollow intervenes between what is in it and other things.

From this it is said of the appointed time: mawqib. And awqabahu: he imprisoned him or destroyed him.

Among its hamzated (mahmuz) forms: أبِقَ العَبْدُ (abiqa al-'abdu, "the slave ran away"), like سَمِعَ, ضَرَبَ and مَنَعَ, with the verbal noun أبْقًا (abqan). It may also be vocalized as أَبَقًا (abaqan) with a fatha on the first letter, with the verbal noun وإباقًا (ibaqan), vocalized like كِتابٍ (kitab). It means he went off without fear or exertion of effort, or he hid himself and then went off. All of this returns to the notion of making him as if he had descended into a وقْبَة (waqba, a cavity or hole), and it is in his nature then to hide.

From the same root: تَأبَّقَ (ta'abbaqa) means he concealed himself or was detained. تَأبَّقَ الشَّيْءَ (ta'abbaqa al-shay') means he denied the thing, because the cause of denial is concealment. تَأبَّقَ (ta'abbaqa) also means تَأثَّمَ (ta'athtama), he avoided sin, that is, he kept away from the sin. So it is either for the negation of gathering (الجَمْع) or for the negation of perishing in the waqba.

الأبَقُ (al-abaq), vocalized مُحَرَّكَةً (with a vowel on the first letter), means القِنَّبُ (al-qinnab, hemp), because of its resemblance to the waqba in its hollowness. الأبَقُ (al-abaq) also means قِشْرُهُ (qishruhu, its husk or skin), because of its strong binding for gathering, or because it consists of gathered threads.

And when He established what they had with their partners, He mentioned their state in the continuation of their ignorance, so He said, exalted is He: ﴿And the criminals will see the Fire﴿ — that is, those deeply immersed in criminality — ﴿the Fire﴾ — that is, they saw it. But He expressed it this way to indicate that the judgment is tied to the description. ﴿Then they will think﴾ a thought ﴿that they are going to fall into it, and they will not﴾ — that is, while they do not — ﴿find any escape from it﴾ — that is, any place they could turn to. So the context is one of certainty, yet their thinking is, in keeping with their habit of ignorance, as they said: ﴿God has taken a son﴾ [al-Kahf: 4], without knowledge, and ﴿I do not think this will ever perish﴾ [al-Kahf: 35], ﴿nor do I think the Hour will be established﴾ [al-Kahf: 36], ﴿We only assume, and we are not certain﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 32], despite the presence of the evidences, about which there is no doubt.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 54:

Since the discourse was, in effect, saying: "We have varied these reports with the great secrets they point to, so the majestic proofs of the Sharia stood firm, and by them the shining essences of meanings were illuminated," it follows this with: ﴿And We have certainly varied﴾, that is, by the greatness We possess. Since this surah is about describing the Book, the concern for it required placing it first in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿in this Qur'an﴾, that is, the upright one in which there is no crookedness, combining meanings and spreading out what distinguishes between confusing matters, ﴿for the people﴾, that is, those who are shaken, let alone those who are firm, ﴿from every example﴾, that is, We turned the speech around and approached it from every aspect of the meanings, and clothed it in refined expressions and harmonious styles, such that, in its strangeness, it travelled like a proverb: everyone who hears it accepts it, and it is carried by the camels' flanks through all the lands among the servants, so their hearts rejoice in it and their tongues repeat it. Yet they did not accept it and they argued about it. Then he drew attention to the quality that calls for this, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But man has been most of anything argumentative﴾, the one who was made a disputant, though he is most at ease with himself by nature and disposition. He distinguished the "most" by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿in dispute﴾, because he did not desist from disputation after this clarification, which illuminated all the created worlds.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 55:

When he (Allah) had explained their aversion, He explained its cause in their view, saying: ﴿And what prevented﴾ Since people followed Quraysh, He said: ﴿the people﴾, i.e., those who disputed with falsehood, from ﴿believing﴾ in faith. This was the original form, but He expressed this second object by His words, exalted is He, ﴿that they believe﴾, to convey renewal and to censure them for abandoning it, ﴿when﴾, i.e., at the time when ﴿the guidance﴾ came to them through the Book upon the tongue of the Messenger. He coordinated with the second object, expressing it with the same form as what preceded for what preceded, His words, exalted is He, ﴿and that they seek forgiveness from their Lord﴾, i.e., the One who is good to them.

Since the exception is incomplete (mufarragh), He brought the agent, so He said, exalted is He: ﴿except that﴾, i.e., they await that ﴿the way of the former peoples should come upon them﴾ in response to their agreeing to what they proposed to their messengers, which necessitates annihilation for whoever persists in error. Among this is their request that the Prophet be an angel, and that is a vengeance in the form of a blessing, and the coming of punishment from behind (dubur), i.e., concealed. ﴿Or﴾ they await that ﴿the punishment should come upon them face to face (qubulan)﴾, i.e., openly, directly and visibly, without any concealment of it. In the reading of the one who kissed the qaf and opened the ba', it is clear, from their saying: "I met so-and-so qibalan," i.e., face to face. Likewise in the reading of the one who vocalized both with a damma, from their saying: "I come to you qubulan, not dubur," i.e., facing you, from the direction of your face and not from the direction of your back. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿If his shirt is torn from the front (min qubul)﴾ [Yusuf: 26]. It is also valid that this reading means the category, because the intended punishment is the genus, i.e., it comes to them in classes, each class and each kind separately, and its explanation has passed in al-An'am. This second part is the counterpart of the coming of the way of the former peoples, so its meaning is: without their being granted what they proposed, as has preceded in the one before it. ﴿But most people refused except disbelief﴾ [al-Isra': 89]. ﴿And they said: We will never believe you﴾ [al-Isra': 90], up to His words, exalted is He: ﴿or you cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claimed﴾ [al-Isra': 92], and this verse is of ihtibak: mentioning ﴿the way of the former peoples﴾ first indicates its opposite second, and mentioning the disclosure second indicates the concealment first.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 56:

Since that is not up to the Messenger, but rather up to the Deity, He explained it with His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We do not send﴾ — by virtue of the greatness We possess, in which no one has any command alongside Us — ﴿the messengers except as bringers of good tidings﴾ of good for acts of obedience, ﴿and warners﴾ of evil for acts of disobedience. Thus the wrongdoers among their peoples demand of them what is not within their power, of the decisive command (fasl al-amr). ﴿And those who disbelieve dispute by means of falsehood﴾ — that is, they renew the disputation whenever a command comes to them from Our side — ﴿in order to refute﴾ — that is, to make slip, so they remove and nullify — ﴿thereby the truth﴾ — the established truth of the miracles which affirm their truthfulness. Their saying is from their own words: "If you were truthful, you would bring us what we demand from you," although that is not so, because no one other than God has any share of command.

Since every situation has its own speech, and for every speech there is a limit and a state, He used the form of the future in the disputation. And since taking mockery was a single matter, He expressed it in the past tense, saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they took﴾ — that is, they burdened themselves by taking ﴿My signs﴾ — the good tidings, which are the thing intended in itself for every living being — ﴿and that with which they were warned﴾ of My signs, passive voice because the agent is known, and what frightens is the warning — ﴿as a mockery﴾, although the two are very far from that. So they did not obey out of desire, nor were they alarmed out of fear, and so they became worse than the beasts.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 57:

When He related their disputation, their mockery and their misguidance, He described them with that which entails disgrace. He said, linking it to what is implied, meaning: "Thus they were the most wrongdoing of wrongdoers": ﴿And who is more unjust﴾ than them? This is a question in the form of affirmation (taqrir), but He used it to draw attention to the attribute that makes the denial necessary, against anyone who doubts that they are the most unjust. Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿than one who is reminded﴾, that is, by any reminder whatever, "of the signs" (ayat), that is, the indications (ʿalamat) of ﴿his Lord﴾, who has done good to him through them. Al-Asbahani said: "This is among the most eloquent forms of affirmation: that a man be confronted with something to which there is no answer except the one his opponent wants."

Since reminding is a cause of turning toward (the truth), and they reversed this, He said, exalted is He: ﴿So he turned away from them﴾, abandoning what he knows of those wondrous indications and what the [good -] that bestowed them entails of gratitude. ﴿And forgot what his hands had sent forward﴾, of corruption, which he would know, if he turned his intellect to reflection on what benefits him, that wisdom requires his recompense for it. He used the singular pronoun throughout all of this, following the wording of "man" (min), to indicate that whoever does the like of this, even if he is one person, is in this state. The better view is that they, when they had asked the Jews about him, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, as is indicated at ﴿And they ask you about the Spirit﴾ [al-Isra 17:85], and they told them to ask him about what they had made a sign of his truthfulness, and this did not affect them. They persisted in denial after he informed them of the truth. He explained their condition by sequencing with the particle fa (then/so), and the meaning is: "Who is more unjust than them?" Because they were reminded and turned away, and forgot what they had believed to be the proof of truth, and that there is no dispute after it. The purpose of the particle fa at the end of the prostration (sajdah) will come with further explanation.
