Attributing the verb of turning away and what follows it to them is literal, by what they have of [acquisition (kasb) -], just as attributing the making and what follows it to God is literal, by what He has of [creation (khalq)].

Since it was as if it were said: "What is wrong with them that they did this? Does anyone fail to know the ugliness of this?" It was said: (p-93) ﴿Indeed, We have placed﴾, by what We have of power to blind insights and sights, ﴿over their hearts﴾. He gathered (the pronoun) back to the style of ﴿and they took My signs﴾ [al-Kahf 18:56], because it is more explicit in condemning each one. ﴿Coverings (akinnah)﴾, that is, veils placed over them with a height whose context of majesty indicates that it does not let any good reach them, so they understand nothing of Our signs. By the masculine pronoun in the plural, he indicated that the intended "signs" is the Qur'an. So He said, exalted is He: ﴿lest they understand it﴾, that is, lest they comprehend it, ﴿and in their ears is a deafness (waqr)﴾, that is, a heaviness, so they do not hear with true hearing and do not grasp with true grasping. ﴿And if you call them﴾, that is, you repeatedly call them at every time ﴿to guidance﴾, so that you might save them by what you have of eagerness and earnestness in that, ﴿they will never be guided﴾, that is, all of them because of your calling, ﴿then (idhan)﴾, that is, if you call them, ﴿ever (abadan)﴾. Because He to whom belongs complete majesty, who when He speaks of Himself with the plural of "We" it is in its reality, judged them to be misguided. That is, calling alone does not guide most of them; rather, the sword must accompany it, as We shall command you, so that you cut off heads and the others are humbled. It may also be that the intended meaning is that whoever is like this, stubbornly opposed in this manner, is eternally wretched. And (in) the end of this verse He negated the act from the servants and affirmed it for them at its beginning. We rarely find in the Qur'an a verse that attributes an act to them without another verse accompanying it that affirms it to God and negates it from them, as a trial from God for His servants, so that the firmly grounded may be distinguished, the one who attributes to the responsible persons the acquisition that yields the effect of obligation, and to God the creation, which is beneficial because He, glory be to Him, has no partner in creation or in anything else, from the frivolous one who holds either determinism (jabr) or delegation (tafwid).

When this required their seizure, he linked to the context's required cause, which I mentioned, the words of the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord﴾. By this name he indicated the kindness that the attribute requires, in seizing some of them and granting respite to others, for a wisdom in its final outcome. Then he described Him with the attributes that fit this, saying: ﴿the All-Forgiving﴾, meaning He alone is the one who covers sins, either by erasing them or by forbearing with them until a time. ﴿Full of mercy﴾, meaning [He who -] deals, while being able, with the causes of wrath as a merciful one deals, with honor. Then he cited as evidence for this the words of the Exalted: ﴿If He were to seize them﴾, meaning these people who opposed you and harmed you, while He knows they will not believe, if He dealt with them as one who seizes ﴿for what they earned﴾ at the time of their earning, ﴿He would have hastened the punishment for them﴾ one after another. But He does not hasten it for them; ﴿rather, for them there is an appointed time﴾ at which He will bring it upon them. He indicated, by his saying, showing the perfection of His power, that His appointed time is not like the appointed time of others who are powerless: ﴿They will never find besides Him﴾, [i.e., the appointed time,] ﴿any refuge﴾, meaning a shelter that saves them from it. So when their appointed time comes, We destroy them therein for their first and last wrongdoing.

Since this has been His way with the earlier generations and the bygone peoples, He, exalted, said, linking it to His saying ﴿They have an appointed time﴾ [al-Kahf: 58], and striking fear into them by pointing to their dwellings, which depict their destruction: ﴿And those towns﴾, namely the past ones, of ʿAd, Thamud, Madyan, the people of Lut, and their like, ﴿We destroyed when they wronged﴾, meaning We decreed their destruction by virtue of Our greatness, ﴿when they wronged﴾, meaning at the very first time they wronged, or We destroyed them in actuality when they wronged, but not at its beginning. Rather, We granted them respite until it reached its culmination and its utmost limit, so let these take warning from the like of that. ﴿And We appointed﴾, meaning by virtue of Our greatness, ﴿for their destruction﴾, meaning their actual destruction, ﴿an appointed time﴾, meaning a time at which We would bring it upon them, and a place We would not fail. Just as We appointed for these an appointed time in this world, on the day of Badr, the conquest, Hunayn and the like, and in the Hereafter We will not fail it. Likewise, every matter that a prophet says on Our behalf does not involve failure, though it is permissible for Us to do so. This is unlike what he says from himself, not attributed to Us, for failure may occur in it, as occurred in the promise of informing about these matters, the delay of forty nights or less, according to their understanding that "tomorrow" is literal. (p-96)

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 60:

When he (Allah) had presented the discourse on resurrection (al-ba'th), and argued for it from the beginning of creation, then mentioned some of its circumstances, then followed that with the parables He struck for it and for other things, and turned through the aspects of argumentation, and concluded all of that by stating that He grants respite at the time of harm, He followed that by stating that He likewise acts at the time of joy: "For everything there is a Book with Him, and every decree is by measure and reckoning." Thus He mentioned the story of Musa with al-Khidr, peace be upon them both, and what befell him in his quest, and His (glorified is He) making the fish a sign and an appointed meeting for their encounter. Had He (glorified is He) willed, He could have brought the distance near and not caused him toil, along with what it contains of the extraordinary that indicates resurrection, and of the proof that whoever's virtue and knowledge are established may not be opposed except by one who is certain of what he says from his Lord, nor be tested. It also contains guidance to condemning disputation without knowledge, and to the obligation of submitting to the truth when it is explained and its proof becomes manifest. It also contains guidance for one who disdains to sit with the poor among the believers: that Musa, peace be upon him, who is the interlocutor of Allah, followed al-Khidr, peace be upon him, in order to acquire some of his knowledge. It also contains a rebuke to the Jews for their saying to the Quraysh, when they instructed them to ask the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant him peace, "If he does not inform you, then he is not a prophet," which gives the Arabs, who know nothing, the impression that it is a condition of a prophet that nothing be hidden from him, even though they know that Musa, peace be upon him, was unaware of all that al-Khidr, peace be upon him, did. To something similar al-Khidr, peace be upon him, alluded in his saying, when a sparrow alighted on the edge of the ship and pecked one or two pecks from the sea: "My knowledge and your knowledge, O Musa, do not diminish the knowledge of Allah except as much as this sparrow diminishes from the sea." It also contains, by informing them of what they know, that Musa, peace be upon him, made himself a follower of al-Khidr, peace be upon him, as a refutation of their claim that no one is superior to Musa, peace be upon him, in any attribute, and that it is not fitting for anyone to follow other than him. And it contains, as an answer to what they may say to the Arabs out of slander and envy, "Had he been a prophet, he would not have said, 'I will inform you tomorrow,' and he would not have delayed in that," by what befell Musa in his promise to al-Khidr, peace be upon them both, to be patient, and by what was hidden from him of what al-Khidr, peace be upon them both, had been made aware of.

Then He (exalted is He), continuing on His saying (glorified is He) "And when We said to the angels" [al-Kahf: 50], said: "And when" — that is, and mention to them the time when "Musa said" — that is, the son of Imran, the one sent to the Children of Israel — that is, his saying which was at that time, "to his young man" — Yusha' ibn Nun, peace be upon them both: "I will not cease" — that is, I will not cease traveling in pursuit of the servant whom my Lord has informed me of, for his virtue, as what follows indicates — "until I reach the meeting place of the two seas" (p-98), that is, their junction and the place of their mixing, which my understanding had reached, so that starting with it was determined, and I shall find him there. "Or I will proceed for a long period" if I do not attain the meeting place of the two seas which my Lord has made an appointment for me in meeting him. And the ḥuqub — as stated in al-Qamus — is eighty years or more, and the age or years. End of quotation. How fitting is the appointed meeting at the junction of the two seas of water with the junction of the two seas of knowledge, and their provisioning with the nun that Allah joined with the pen and what they write, and the Fountain of Life, because knowledge is the life of hearts. So they journeyed on, and took with them a roasted fish in a basket, as they had been commanded, and they kept eating from it until they reached the junction.

**Qur'an 18:61:** ﴿So when they reached the meeting-place of the two﴾, i.e., the two seas, and there was no barrier there at all, since the two had become one thing. ﴿They forgot their fish﴾. Musa, peace be upon him, therefore knew nothing of its condition and forgot to ask about it, while Yusha' (Joshua), peace be upon him, knew some of its condition but forgot to mention it to him. ﴿So it took﴾, i.e., the fish, a miracle within a miracle, ﴿its path﴾, i.e., its wide and clear way, ﴿into the sea in a tunnel﴾, i.e., an opening in the water that did not close, from the word *sarab*, which is the burrow of a wild animal, an underground hollow, or a conduit through which water enters a wall. It has been reported in a hadith in the Sahih (the authentic collection) that God Most High restored it to life and held back the place where it moved through the water, so it became an arch that did not close. Yusha', peace be upon him, was watching that, and it seems the meeting-place extended, so Musa, peace be upon him, thought that what he sought was ahead of him, or he thought that the intended meeting-place was another one, and so he set off.

**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 62:**

﴿When they had passed beyond it﴾, that is, when Musa and his servant (peace be upon them both) had passed that place of the meeting of the two seas, he became weary. He had not felt weariness until he had passed the place he had been commanded to reach, as another miracle. So when he became hungry and weary, ﴿he said to his servant: "Bring us our morning meal"﴾, that is, bring us our food, ﴿so that we may be strengthened by it﴾ against the exhaustion that had befallen us. For this reason, he joined to it his saying, may He be exalted: ﴿"We have indeed suffered fatigue from this journey of ours"﴾, that is, the journey we had traveled on this very day in particular. For this reason he pointed to it with the demonstrative of proximity (ism al-isharah li'l-qurb), so He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿"this"﴾ [i.e., this journey] ﴿"fatigue"﴾. The fish had been their provision, so it was not with him. It is as if it were said: "What was the matter with it (the fish)?" So it was said:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 63:

﴿He said﴾ to Musa, pewhich peace be upon him, expressing wonder at him: ﴿Did you see﴾ what afflicted me, ﴿when we took refuge at the rock﴾ that is at the meeting place of the two seas? ﴿Indeed I﴾ meaning [because I] ﴿forgot the fish﴾, meaning I forgot to mention to you its matter that had happened there. Then he increased the wonder at this forgetting by inserting, between reporting it in summary and detailing its matter, and by attributing the forgetting to it and then to the mention of it, so He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And none made me forget it﴾, despite its being a marvel, ﴿except Satan﴾ through his whisperings.

Since the context is one of training in the great control of Allah, the Exalted, [over the hearts] by establishing knowledge and negating it, even though it is necessary knowledge, He mentioned his forgetting. Then He substituted from its pronoun (p-100) the words of the Exalted: ﴿that I should mention it﴾ to you. For it had come alive, and slipped away from the basket into the sea, ﴿and it took its way﴾, meaning its path by which it went, ﴿into the sea in a wondrous manner﴾. Its mention to him now prevents it from being that Satan had authority over it, on the basis that this causing to forget did not cause them to miss an act of obedience. Rather, in it was an elevation for both of them through the ascending stages of the lofty ranks, by their finding fatigue after the place where the goal lay, and the preservation of the water flowing away over a long time, and other signs of certainty. The words of the Exalted ﴿His authority is only over those who take him as an ally﴾ [al-Nahl: 100] make clear that authority means enticing toward disobedience. In this story there were extraordinary events: the fish's life, the restoration of what had been eaten of it, and the holding back of the water from its entry place. Something similar has also occurred to our Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, himself or his followers by his blessing.

As for the restoration of what had been eaten of the roasted fish, which was its side, al-Bayhaqi narrated at the end of Dala'il al-Nubuwwa from Usama ibn Zayd, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "We went out with the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, on the pilgrimage he performed, until when we were at Batn al-Rawha' [he mentioned the story of the woman whose son the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, cured of madness, until he said]: When the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, had completed his pilgrimage, he departed until, when he alighted at Batn al-Rawha' (p-101), that woman came to him with a sheep she had roasted. He ordered that the sheep be taken from her, then said: 'O Usaym!' – and when he called him he used the diminutive form of his name – 'Pass me a foreleg!' And the most beloved part of the sheep to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, was its front. Then he said: 'O Usaym! Pass me a foreleg!' So I passed it to him. Then he said: [O Usaym! Pass me a foreleg! I said: O Messenger of Allah! They are only two forelegs, and I have passed them to you. He said]: 'By Him in whose hand is my soul, if you had been silent, you would have kept passing me a foreleg, and I would not have said to you: Pass me a foreleg!'" [So he, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, informed that if he had been silent] Allah would have produced for her a foreleg, then another foreleg, and so on. His word is the truth, with no difference between what is in the unseen world and what is found in the visible world.

As for the life of the roasted fish, what is greater than that has already passed at the verse ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67], in the story of the poisoned roasted sheep, namely that its foreleg informed the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, [that it was poisoned]. That is greater than the return of life without speech. Likewise the trunk's yearning, the stone's greeting, the pebbles' glorification, the lintel of the door and the walls of the house (p-102) affirming and similar things are greater than the return of life to what was living. Al-Bayhaqi narrated in al-Dala'il from Amr ibn Sawad, who said: al-Shafi'i said to me: "Allah did not give any prophet what He gave Muhammad, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace." I said: "Did He not give 'Isa, peace be upon him, the raising of the dead?" He said: "He gave Muhammad, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, the trunk, which he used to lean on while preaching beside it, until a pulpit was prepared for him. When the pulpit was prepared for him, the trunk yearned until its sound was heard." This is greater than that. End quote. Moreover, there has already been mention, in Al 'Imran and at the end of al-Baqarah, in the story of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, of things concerning the raising of the dead for him, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, and for some of his community.

As for the sign of the water, its return is to its hardness. There is no difference between its stillness through not rejoining after being split, and its stillness and hardness through refraining from being split. Al-Bayhaqi narrated concerning this what contains a sign of revival, with an interrupted chain of narration (p-103), from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "We were in the Suffa with the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, when a woman [who had emigrated] came to him with her son [who had reached maturity]. He hosted the woman with the women and hosted her son with us. Not long after, the plague of Madina struck him, and he fell ill for some days, then died. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, closed his eyes and ordered his preparation for burial. [When] we wanted to wash him, he said: 'Go to his mother and inform her.' She came and sat at his feet, took hold of them, and said: 'O Allah, I have submitted to You willingly, I have renounced the idols out of asceticism, and I have emigrated to You out of desire. O Allah, [do not let the idol-worshippers rejoice over me, and do not burden me with this calamity beyond what I can bear.]' He said: 'By Allah, her words had not ended before he moved his feet and threw the cloth from his face, and he lived until Allah took His Messenger, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, and until his mother died.'" Then Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, equipped an army, and he appointed al-'Ala' ibn al-Hadrami over it. [Anas] said: "I was on his campaign. We arrived at our destinations and found the enemy had gone ahead of us and had covered the water traces. [He said:] The heat was intense, and thirst and our animals distressed us. That was a Friday. When the sun declined toward its setting, he prayed two rak'as with us, then he stretched out his hand, while we saw nothing in the sky. By Allah, he had not lowered his hand before Allah sent a wind and produced a cloud, which poured down until it filled the pools and ravines. We drank, gave drink to our animals, and filled our water containers (p-104). Then we came to our enemy, who had crossed a creek in the sea to an island. He stood at the creek and said: 'O Ali, O Great, O Forbearing, O Generous!' Then he said: 'Cross in the name of Allah!' We crossed what only the water wetting our animals' hooves reached. We caught the enemy unawares, killed, captured and took prisoners. Then we came to the creek, and he said the same words, and we crossed what only the water wetting our animals' hooves reached." And Abu al-Husayn ibn Bishran informed us: Isma'il al-Saffar related to us: al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Affan related to us [from] Ibn Numayr, from al-A'mash, from some of his companions, who said: "We reached the Tigris, which was in flood, and the non-Arabs were behind it. A man among the Muslims said: 'In the name of Allah,' then he urged his horse forward and it advanced over the water. The people said: 'In the name of Allah, in the name of Allah,' then they plunged in and rose over the water. When the non-Arabs saw them, they said: 'Diwan! Diwan!' and fled headlong. They lost nothing except a cup that had hung from the tassel of a saddle. When they came out, they obtained booty and divided it." Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami informed us: Abu Muhammad 'Abd Allah ibn Muhammad al-Simadhi related to us: Abu al-'Abbas al-Sarraj related to us: al-Fadl ibn Sahl and Harun ibn 'Abd Allah related to us, both said: Sulayman ibn al-Mughira related to us that Abu Muslim al-Khawlani came to the Tigris, which was carrying wood with its flood, so he walked on the water, turned to his companions and said: "Do you miss anything of your goods (p-105), so that we may call upon Allah?" Al-Bayhaqi said: This chain is sound.

In this matter of this story there is a crushing rebuke to the questioners and to those who instructed them to ask, because the intended meaning, and Allah knows best, is that this event happened to the prophet of these misguided people. So let them command Quraysh to ask them about this story. If the people of the Book inform them of it in the same way you informed them, and they confirm it, then they are bound to believe in resurrection, because of this fish that Allah brought back to life after it had been roasted and much of it had been eaten. If they do not confirm it in this matter but confirm them in other matters by which they seek to trouble you, then this is arbitrary choice. If they accuse them in every matter, then their asking them is pointless and is not among the actions of a person who has sense.

It is as if it was said: "What did Moses say then?" And it was said: ﴿He said﴾, drawing attention to the fact that this was not from Satan, but was an inattention from Allah, exalted is He, without an intermediary, so that they would find the sign with which Allah had informed him, just as the Prophet (ﷺ) said, may the peace and blessings of Allah be upon him and his family: "Indeed I forget, that is, Allah causes me to forget, so that I may establish a precedent."

﴿That﴾, that is, the great matter of the loss of the fish, ﴿is what we were seeking﴾ (p-106), that is, what we wanted of this hidden matter that was concealed from us, for Allah, exalted is He, made it an appointment for me to meet al-Khidr. ﴿So they turned back, retracing their footsteps﴾, relating them, ﴿tracing their path﴾. This indicates that the land was sand with no landmarks. The apparent meaning, and Allah knows best, is that it was the confluence of the Nile and the salt water near Damietta or Rashid in the lands of Egypt. This is supported by the sparrow pecking at the sea in the boat in which they had sailed, for nourishment, as in the hadith, for a bird does not drink from salt water. It is well known in the lands of Rashid that this matter was known among them, and that they have a fish with a split side, and they say it is from the offspring of that fish, and Allah knows best.

So they continued relating the path until they reached the place where the fish had been lost.

﴿So they found a servant of Our servants﴾, one attached to the presence of Our greatness, and he was al-Khadir (Khidr, peace be upon him). ﴿We had given him﴾ by Our greatness “mercy”, that is, revelation and prophethood. That he was a prophet is the view of the majority (al-jumhur) of scholars. “From Our presence” means from that which does not proceed according to the laws of customary means, although this is not strange to the people of election (ahl al-istifa’). ﴿And We had taught him from Our own presence﴾, that is, from the hidden and strange matters that are with Us, which do not arise from the customary causes. Thus it is strange to the people of election. ﴿Knowledge﴾ which We cast into his heart without an intermediary.

[And] Ustadh Abu al-Hasan al-Harrali said: “‘Inda” in the language of the Arabs is for what is apparent, and “ladun” is for what is inward. So the intended meaning of “mercy” is the manifest acts of grace (karamat) from Him, and the intended meaning of “knowledge” is the inward, hidden knowledge, known with certainty to be specific to His sacred presence. The Sufis (ahl al-tasawwuf, the mystics) called knowledge acquired through the path of unveiling (al-mukashafa) “ladunni knowledge” (the knowledge from His presence). When the servant strives in the spiritual exercises (al-riyadiyyat), the outward self is adorned with worship, the soul is emptied of blameworthy traits, and is adorned with praiseworthy traits. The sensory, imaginative and estimative faculties reach the utmost strength, [and at that point the rational faculty becomes strong -] pure [and perhaps the soul, by its original natural disposition, is luminous, divine, lofty, and little attached -] to bodily events, and highly prepared to receive divine matters. Then divine lights shine upon it and pour into it from the world of holiness in perfect form, so that knowledge and insights are attained without reflection or contemplation. This is ladunni knowledge.

(p. 107)

Then Allah, glorified and exalted be He, presented the story as a fresh statement (istiʾnaf), as though answering a questioner about every utterance that the preceding material points to. It is known that a seeker who meets a person speaks to him, but the exact wording of that speech is not specified. So He said, to one who is as if he had asked about it: ﴿Moses said to him﴾, requesting of him, by way of courtesy and gentleness, expressed in the form of seeking permission: ﴿May I follow you﴾, that is, follow you with eloquent following wherever you go. Ittibaʿ (following) is coming to do what another does, merely because one is coming to it with him. He made clear that he asks of him nothing but knowledge, saying: ﴿on condition that you teach me﴾ (p-108). He increased the gentleness by indicating that he does not ask for all that is with him, lest the time be prolonged for him, but rather for comprehensive parts through which he may be guided to the rest. So He said: ﴿of what you have been taught﴾. It is in the passive form because those addressed know, being sincere ones, that the agent is Allah, glorified and exalted be He, and to indicate the ease of every matter for Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿right guidance (rushdan)﴾, that is, knowledge that guides me to the right course in what I intend. There is no deficiency in one prophet learning from another, so as to claim that this Moses is not Moses son of ʿImran, peace be upon him, for it has been established in the authentic reports that he is the son of ʿImran. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, in his request of him, used these kinds of courtesies and exceeding humility, in keeping with his firm rootedness in knowledge; for everyone whose grasp of the sciences is greater, his knowledge of what they contain of delight and happiness is greater, so his desire for them is more intense, and his veneration of the masters of knowledge is more complete.

When he had finished stating the question, he began his answer to it with his saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said﴾, that is, al-Khidr, peace be upon him: ﴿"Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me,"﴾ O Musa, ﴿"patience"﴾, that is, it is, by reason of its greatness, of the kind I undertake, because of what urges you towards not being patient, namely the outward aspects of the Sharia in which you have been commanded [to act]. The tanwin (indefinite ending) here is for magnification, as the form of the verb with the t of the tafa'ul pattern (تَسْتَطِيعَ) indicates, and it is more emphatic, because of the gentleness in Musa's question, which indicates that he would be patient with him and would not oppose him in anything at all. From this it is derived that if a scholar sees that harshness towards the student would benefit him and guide him to good, it is incumbent upon him to mention it, for silence about it leads the student into delusion and conceit, and that prevents him from learning.

Now when the situation was extremely difficult, since it concerned the commands of God Most High, He explained it in a manner more eloquent than negating the more specific, namely eloquent patience, by expressing wonder at patience in general [as an absolute], excusing Moses for his denial and Himself for the act, on the ground that this pertains to the outward and the inward. So He said, linking it to what is implied by the context: "How then will you follow me with the eloquent following?" ﴿And how can you be patient﴾ O Moses ﴿regarding that which you do not encompass in knowledge﴾, that is, from the standpoint of knowing it outwardly and inwardly. By the word "encompass" He indicated that it was possible for it to be correct, but only as a supposition that does not remove from him the obligation of the command. It is also possible that this is a justification for what came before it, so the second patience would be the first, and the meaning would be: you are not able to have the patience that I intend, because you do not know my act as it truly is, so that you would see it as corrupt.

Said [Musa], peace be upon him, displaying the utmost humility before one who is more knowledgeable than him, as guidance on what is fitting in seeking knowledge, hoping that Allah would facilitate it for him and make him benefit from it: ﴿You will find me﴾, so he emphasized the promise with the particle sin (the future marker, i.e. "soon" or "surely"). Then Allah, glorified is He, informed about him that he reinforced this emphasis by seeking blessing through mentioning Allah, the Exalted, knowing the difficulty of the matter, in the manner that was previously urged in this surah, in His saying, ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow"﴾ [al-Kahf: 23], etc., so that it would be known that this is the method of the prophets and the path of the messengers. Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿If Allah wills﴾, i.e., He who possesses the attributes of perfection, ﴿patient﴾ in what it is permissible to be patient with. Then he increased the emphasis with his saying, joined by the conjunction "and" to "patient," to show his firm resolve in each of the two qualities: ﴿and I will not disobey﴾, i.e., and not disobeying, ﴿any order of yours﴾, which you command me, not contravening the apparent command of Allah.

He said: "If you follow me" — O Musa — following him with eloquent following, "then do not ask me about anything" I say or do "until I myself mention to you" specifically "an explanation of it" that makes clear to you the aspect of its correctness. For I do not undertake anything except that it is correct and permissible in reality, even if its outward appearance is otherwise.

When they had agreed on the condition and consented to it, God's words ﴿So they set off﴾ were caused by it. That is, Musa and al-Khidr, peace be upon them both, went along the shore seeking a boat to board, and they kept going ﴿until, when they boarded the boat,﴾ and the answer to the conditional clause is His words ﴿he made a hole in it﴾. He used the definite form for the boat, "the boat," to direct the context back to the mention of the meeting place of the two seas, indicating that their setting out [was -] for the purpose of seeking a boat, so that it was as if it were present in the mind for that reason. He did not join "made a hole" with a fa' (of consequence), because it was not caused by the boarding, nor was it at the first of their moments. Then He resumed with His words ﴿He [Musa] said﴾, meaning Musa, peace be upon him, denouncing it because of its apparent corruption, the destruction of property, which leads to a greater corruption, the destruction of lives. [Forgetting -] the solemn covenant he had made with himself, because of what had overwhelmed him from his Lord, who is the Mighty God, namely the firm covenant repeated in all the books of the Torah after its affirmation on the two tablets of testimony in the Ten Commandments, whose relation to the Torah is like the relation of al-Fatihah to the Qur'an, by the definite command that He does not approve of wrongdoing. It is established that the prohibition of wrongdoing is obligatory immediately. Moreover, had he not forgotten, he would not have abandoned denunciation, as he did at the killing of the boy, because such a thing is not included in the promise, since what is excepted by the Sharia is like what is excepted in its wording. So in the first case he forgot the condition, and in the second he forgot, because of what overwhelmed him of the horror of the killing, [about which he did not know -] any command from God, that it was proper to follow him, given God's praise of him: ﴿Have you made a hole in it﴾. He explained his excuse for denouncing it by pointing to the extreme horror of the breach, saying ﴿to drown its people﴾. By Allah! ﴿You have certainly done a grave thing﴾, meaning a great, reprehensible, wondrous and severe thing.

﴿He said﴾, i.e., al-Khidr, peace be upon him: ﴿Did I not tell you that you﴾ O Musa! (p-١١٢) ﴿would never be able to have patience with me﴾? So he reminded him of what he had said to him at the time of the condition.

Moses said, ﴿Do not hold me accountable for what I forgot﴾, O Khidr, ﴿concerning that condition﴾, ﴿and do not burden me﴾ meaning, do not make me reach what I cannot bear, and do not hasten me away from my purpose by following you under compulsion, attributing to me foolishness, levity, and committing wrong, ﴿with difficulty in my affair﴾, by holding me to account for forgetting. So each of them speaks truthfully in what he said and fulfills according to what he has. As for Moses, peace be upon him, it never occurred to him [to him -] to pledge that he would not object to what he believes [to be reprehensible -]. As for Khidr, he made his pledge in accordance with the reality of the matter, since he would not undertake what is reprehensible. Yet, despite this, he did not negate [anything but -] the complete patience which is indicated by the addition of the taa' of al-istif'al (the tā' of the tenth form verbal pattern, ta'alluf-type reflexive/requestive sense), and some of what is called patience was achieved. For when Moses reminded him, he refrained from objecting, because he recalled God's praise of him that he does not do what is false. But the complete patience that was in Khidr's own soul was not achieved by silence at the beginning and at the end of the matter.

﴿So they set off﴾ after they had disembarked from the ship and were safe from drowning and from seizure. ﴿Until, when they met a boy﴾ who had not reached puberty and who was at the peak of strength. ﴿So he killed him﴾ at the moment he met him, as the connecting *al-fāʾ al-ʿāṭifa* (الفاءُ العاطِفَةُ, the "fa" of consequence) indicates, linking it to the condition. He then answered the condition with his words, which imply that his beginning of denunciation in this case was swifter: ﴿He said﴾, that is, Mūsā, peace be upon him: ﴿Have you killed﴾ O Khiḍr ﴿a pure soul﴾ (p-113) in that it remained upon its original natural disposition, without being defiled by a sin that would make killing obligatory, ﴿without a soul﴾ it had killed, so that your killing of it would be *qawad* (قَوَدًا, retaliatory punishment in kind). This indicates that he was an adult, since if he had killed a victim it would have been possible to execute him in return, unless their law does not require puberty as a condition. Then he resumed his speech: ﴿You have certainly done﴾ in your killing of it ﴿a thing﴾, and he made the denunciation explicit in his words ﴿a monstrous thing﴾ because it was direct action [-]. The breaching was a causal act, which does not necessarily entail drowning.

Since this was the second time, [Al-Khidr] (peace be upon him) said: "Did I not tell you" and he added to his statement, "that you," O Musa, "will not be able to have patience with me" — meaning specifically — "patience."

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 76:

﴿Qāla﴾ Mūsā ʿalayhi al-salām, out of shame before Him, when he came to himself after recalling what had taken place from the excess of his ecstatic longing for God's command, and he mentioned that he had only followed him by God's command: ﴿If I ask you about anything after this﴾, O my brother! He made known the intensity of his regret over the denial by saying ﴿then do not keep me company﴾, rather part from me. Then he gave the reason for that by saying ﴿you have reached the excuse from my side﴾, and he indicated that what had happened from him of breaking the condition was among the greatest of the extraordinary matters to which he was compelled, so he said ﴿from my side an excuse﴾, by my objecting twice and your bearing with me in both of them. And God has informed me of the goodness of your state in the abundance of your knowledge.

﴿So they set out﴾ after killing him, ﴿until when they came to the people of a town﴾. Here he expressed it as "town" (qaryah) rather than "city" (madinah), because it is more indicative of blame. The root q-r-y revolves around gathering (jam'), which entails withholding, as was mentioned at the end of Surat Yusuf, peace be upon him. Then he described it in order to show [that] it has a role in the baseness of its people, through the words of the Most High: ﴿they asked them for food﴾. In his words ﴿its people﴾ he used the explicit noun and did not use a pronoun, because the asking for food was [done] by some of those they came to, or each of the coming and the asking [was done] by a different group, but it is not the same group. This is the apparent meaning, because it is the one that accords with custom.

The Imam Abu al-Hasan al-Harrali said in his book Miftah al-Bab al-Muqfal li-Fahm al-Qur'an al-Munzal: The repetition of nouns through explicit use (iẓhār) and pronoun use (iḍmār) is an indication of the depths of understanding in the Qur'an. Know that the occurrence of explicit use and pronoun use in the Qur'anic exposition has two aspects. In one, explicit use comes first, and this is the address to the believers concerning the signs of the horizons; similar to it is the address of creatures to one another, who use no pronoun until they have made the noun explicit. In the second, pronoun use comes first, and this is the address to those who are certain concerning the sign of the souls, which the address of creatures has not reached. So when the exposition is about comprehensiveness, pronoun use comes first: ﴿Say: He is God, One﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 1]. When it is about specificity (ikhtiṣāṣ), explicit use comes first: ﴿God, the Eternal Refuge﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 2]. When a separate exposition returns to it, he uses a pronoun: ﴿He neither begets nor is begotten﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 3], ﴿and there is none equal to Him, anyone﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 4]; i.e., this is the One who is general in His oneness and specified in His eternal self-sufficiency. And when comprehensive exposition follows specificity, comprehension is resumed by resuming explicit use that encompasses, or by a pronoun, or by combining the pronoun and the explicit noun: ﴿O you who believe, do not put yourselves forward before God and His Messenger, and fear God; indeed God is Hearing, Knowing﴾ [al-Hujurat: 1]; ﴿Indeed the seizure of your Lord is severe﴾ [al-Buruj: 12]; ﴿Indeed it is He who originates and repeats﴾ [al-Buruj: 13]; ﴿He is God, other than whom there is no god, Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾ [al-Hashr: 22]. Awareness of what the Qur'anic exposition is specifically characterized by, distinct from human exposition, is among the keys to the doors of understanding; and of this kind, and similar to it, is ﴿they came to the people of a town and asked its people for food﴾: it resumed, for the two who asked for food, an explicit use different from the explicit use for those who were come to. End of quotation. [Al-Subki made the coming [to the town] apply to some, and the asking for food to all, because it is more severe in blaming the people of the town and more indicative of the evil of their nature. And whoever holds the first view is supported by the words of al-Shafi'i in his book al-Risalah, in the chapter on what was revealed of the Book in general terms, meaning the general, and that specificity enters it, and that is after the fifth clarification, in the saying of God, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿until, when they came to the people of a town, they asked its people for food﴾. In this verse is the clearest indication that they did not ask all the people of the town, and there is specificity in it. End of quotation. The explanation of that is that when an indefinite noun is repeated, the second is other than the first; and when a definite noun is repeated, it is usually the same referent.

And since he attributed the coming to the people of the town, its apparent meaning was to encompass all of them. So if it had been said "they asked them for food," the pronoun would have meant the very ones who were come to. When he turned away from that, despite its being more concise, to the explicit noun, especially if we make it indefinite, it was other than the first; otherwise the turning away would have had no purpose. And since the apparent meaning was that the first [attribution] was to all, the second was to some, otherwise it would not be other than it and the turning away would have no purpose.]

﴿But they refused﴾, i.e., as a consequence of their asking for food, the people of the town who were asked refused ﴿to receive them as guests﴾, i.e., to lodge and feed them. So they departed from them. ﴿Then they found in it﴾, i.e., in the town, and he did not say "in them," as a notice that the intent is to describe the town with bad nature, ﴿a wall that was about to fall﴾, i.e., overlooking collapse. Likewise, borrowing the attribute of what has reason for what has no reason, he said: ﴿wanting to collapse﴾, i.e., to fall quickly. So al-Khadir wiped it with his hand, ﴿and he set it up﴾.

When the description of the town and what resulted from it was finished, he answered "if" (idha) with His saying: ﴿[Musa] said﴾, i.e., Musa, peace be upon him, said to him: ﴿If you had wished, you could have taken﴾ [payment] ﴿for it﴾, because nothing from them had reached us, ﴿upon it﴾, i.e., upon the setting up of the wall, ﴿a wage﴾ ﴿that we could eat with it﴾. So he did not object to him this time, since there was nothing here to be denounced. Rather, he brought what follows from it as its fruit in the manner of presentation and consultation, except that it implies a question.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 78:

﴿He said﴾ al-Khidr (peace be upon him): "This" means the time or the question. Since that was the cause of the parting, or its location, he named it by it, as an intensification, and said: ﴿parting between me and you﴾, O Musa, after the two of you had been one single separation, because of their connection, so there was no "between." In reality, it is more than what had connected the two of them of "between," or it is the parting of the disputation that was between us, that is, the parting that the question caused. When this is understood in terms of al-ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which one term is left implicit and the other is stated, and the reader supplies the missing part), its meaning becomes clearer. Its implied sense is: parting between me and you from what you reported, and parting between you and me as I stipulated. This phrase establishes the parting in the most eloquent manner. That is because if the parting between me and you occurs through a barrier that comes between us, then it has occurred from you by way of priority. The reality is that "bayn" (between) is the spread-out empty space that separates two things, and it is divided between them, so the "between" of each of them extends from the midpoint of that space toward it. When something enters that space and separates them, the "between" of each of them becomes attributed to it, because it has become the between of what is attributed to each of the two "betweens," and then their "between" becomes separation, meaning that the "between" of each of them is other than the "between" of the other. As for one who says that the meaning of "this is parting between us" is the removal of separation and the existence of connection, his view is refuted by the fact that the meaning of "this is connection between us" is continuous companionship. If this were also the meaning of that, the meaning of what indicates connection would be identical to the meaning of what indicates separation. God, glorified and exalted is He, has alerted Musa (peace be upon him) — as in the tafsir of al-Isfahani and others — (p-118) to what al-Khidr (peace be upon him) did, in relation to what happened to him, which is the same as that, exactly alike. He alerted him by the breaking of the ship, whose outward appearance is destruction and whose inward reality is salvation from the hand of the usurper [in regard to the chest that was sealed and cast into the river out of fear for him from the tyrannical Pharaoh], so its outward appearance was [destruction], and its inward reality was salvation. And by the killing of the boy, on the basis that he was protected from harm in reality in killing the Egyptian, even though at that time he did not know it, because he had not yet been given prophethood. And by the rebuilding of the wall without wage, for the sake of watering the daughters of Shu'ayb (peace be upon them), without wage, despite his need for it.

Since it is well known how intensely Musa (peace be upon him) longed to understand the inner reality of these matters, he answered his question, saying: ﴿I will inform you﴾, O Musa, with a promise that will not fail, an important information ﴿of the interpretation﴾, that is, of the return ﴿of that over which you could not have patience﴾, because it contradicted the wisdom you had, [toward the wisdom —]. This is that when two harms conflict, it is necessary to commit the lesser to avert the greater, on the condition that the harm is certain. He wrote the tā' of the Istif'al form here and in what preceded it, to inform that he (p-119) negated only the eloquent capacity for patience, pointing to the difficulty of what Musa bore from that, not the absolute capacity for patience.

﴿As for the boat﴾, which belonged to [its people -] and which I damaged, ﴿it belonged to poor men﴾. This is evidence for al-Shafi'i (the jurist al-Shafi'i) that the faqir (the one in need) is in a worse condition than the miskin (the destitute), because these men owned a boat ("working at sea") so that they could use it to support their livelihood.

Since the damaging was done by Him, He attributed it to Himself alone, out of courtesy toward Allah the Exalted, saying: ﴿I wished to damage it﴾. The loss of its use for a part of a day and the burden on its people of a plank to plug it were less harmful than their losing its benefit entirely, both in its taking and in its being seized by the king. I did not intend to drown its people, as is most immediately understood. Then he joined to that the reason for his action, saying: ﴿and behind them﴾, meaning in front of them. [Perhaps -] he expressed it with the word "behind" (wara') as a metaphor for encompassing the authority of the command in every direction, "they hid it" (warrathum) and "they concealed it" (wawaraw-ha). Al-Harrali (the commentator al-Harrali) explained it in [Surat al-Baqarah] as meaning "behind them" in their unawareness of it, even though it was in front of them in their direction, because he explained "behind" (al-waraa') as what the senses and knowledge cannot reach, wherever the place may be. He said: "It may well happen that a thing is both behind, in that it is not known, and in front, in place."

﴿A king who was seizing﴾ at that time ﴿every boat﴾ that had no defect in it, ﴿by force﴾ from its owners, and its owners had no knowledge of it.

(p-120) Since each of the seizing of boats and the poverty was a cause of the act, he put it [the poverty] before the seizing, indicating that the stronger of the two causes moving him to the act was compassion for the poor. ﴿As for the boy﴾, meaning the one I killed, ﴿his parents were believers﴾, and he himself was sealed upon disbelief, as will come in the hadith of Ubayy, may Allah be pleased with him.

Since it was possible in the sight of al-Khidr, peace be upon him, that this boy, despite his disbelief in himself, would be a cause of his parents' disbelief if he grew up, and since Allah's command to him to kill him was like the act of one who fears that, he attributed the act to both of them in His saying: ﴿so we feared that he would overwhelm them﴾, meaning that he would overcome them and afflict them if he grew up, through their love for him or through his boldness and harshness, ﴿with rebellion﴾, meaning transgression in wrongdoing and excess in it, ﴿and disbelief﴾ toward their blessing, so that he would corrupt their worldly life; or their love for him would lead them to rebellion and disbelief in Allah by obedience to him, so that he would corrupt their religion. Muslim related in al-Qadar, Abu Dawud in al-Sunnah, and al-Tirmidhi in (p-121) al-Tafsir, from Ibn Abbas, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The boy whom al-Khidr killed was sealed as a disbeliever, and had he lived he would have overwhelmed his parents with rebellion and disbelief." This hadith is [the basis of] "Allah knows best what they would have done" [Qur'an 18:80 in the sense of this commentary], which indicates that punishment, in the case of what would have occurred had its condition been met, only applies to what is innate and natural, not to what is accidental; otherwise both parents would be punished on the assumption that the disbelief known of them is what would occur.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 81:

When he mentioned what would follow, on the assumption that the boy remained alive, of corruption, he made his saying the consequence of it: ﴿So We intended﴾, that is, by killing him and relieving the two of them of his evil. Since the replacement for this boy was from God alone, He attributed the action to Himself in His saying: ﴿that their Lord would replace them﴾, that is, the one who does good to them by giving and taking, ﴿with one better than him in purity﴾, in purity and blessing, [i.e. -] in terms of the fact that he was apparent in purity at present, whereas in the outcome, had he lived, he would have been evil and manifestly wicked. This replacement may be patience, and it may be another boy, and this is the one reported, and that she was a girl, ﴿and nearer in mercy﴾, in dutifulness towards them, tenderness toward them, and compassion for them. So the harm that befell them through grieving over him was less than the harm that would have befell them when he grew up, through corrupting their religion or their worldly affairs. (p-122)

﴿And as for the wall﴾, concerning which you indicated taking a wage for it, ﴿it belonged to two young boys﴾, and he indicated that they were below the age of maturity by his saying ﴿orphans﴾.

Since the village (qaryah) does not preclude being called a city (madinah), and since the expression "village" in the first place was more fitting, because it is derived from the meaning of gathering (jam'), it was more fitting for blame over the refusal of hospitality, as it implies their stinginess while gathered together and their love of assembling and hoarding. The word "city" (madinah) carries the meaning of residence, so using it was more fitting, as it indicates that people reside in it. Thus the wall would collapse while they were residing there, and they would take the treasure. He said ﴿in the city﴾, and therefore ﴿I repaired it, seeking reward﴾. ﴿Beneath it was a treasure﴾, that is, wealth stored up ("lahuma," for them both), which, had it fallen, would have been more likely to be lost. ﴿Their father was righteous﴾, so his care was to be upheld, and his offspring were to be left in goodness.

Since reaching the age of maturity (bulugh) and extracting the treasure were the act of Allah alone, it was attributed to Him specifically. He said ﴿so your Lord willed﴾, that is, the One who does good to you through this upbringing, indicating what He had done for you of the like before prophethood, as was explained. ﴿That they reach their maturity﴾, that is, the two boys, ﴿their full strength﴾, that is, their sound judgment and their strength. ﴿And that they extract their treasure﴾ so that they may benefit from it and benefit the righteous, ﴿as a mercy﴾ upon them ﴿from your Lord﴾, (p-123) that is, the One who nurtured you well while you were in the status of an [orphan]. So the labor of repairing the wall, done without payment, was less harmful than the necessary harm of its collapse, which would lose the treasure and ruin the wall. This indicates that the righteousness of fathers calls for care for their children. It is related from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said to one of the Kharijites [in a discussion] that took place between them: "By what did Allah preserve the treasure of the two boys?" He said: "By the righteousness of their father." He said: "Then my father and my grandfather are better than him." He said: "Allah has informed us that you are a quarrelsome people."

﴿And I did not do it﴾, that is, any of that, ﴿of my own accord﴾, but by the command of the One to whom the command belongs, who is Allah.

When the secret of those matters became clear, he said, estimating the matter: "That" (dhalika), that is, the great explanation, ﴿is the interpretation of that which you could not bear with patience﴾, O Musa, ﴿patiently﴾. He omitted the ta' of ability (in "tastati'") here, because that matter, after the veil was lifted, falls within what can be borne. So whoever denies it would not have been patient at all had it been unveiled to him from the outset. And there falls away, praise be to Allah, through what has been established in this narrative, what is said: that the Prophet (ﷺ) reported in the saying of Sulayman (peace be upon him), recorded in the two Sahihs from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him: "I will go around tonight to a hundred women, each of whom will bear a horseman [who will strive] in the way of Allah." But only one of them bore, and she bore half a human being. [He said that] had he said "if Allah wills," they would have all fought as horsemen. This makes clear that every prophet who made an exception in his report, Allah confirmed it, as happened with the sacrificed one (al-Dhabih), who said: ﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, among the patient﴾ [al-Saffat: 102], and he fulfilled it. So what did Musa (peace be upon him), who is among the Ulu al-'Azm (the resolute messengers), do with the exception that he did? The sacrificed one was patient with what he was certain was precisely the command of Allah, unlike Musa (peace be upon him), who used to deny what outwardly appeared to be wrong before knowing that it was from the command of Allah. When he was reminded, he was patient. As for the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "May Allah have mercy on my brother Musa! We wished that he had been patient until we were told more about their affair," its meaning is: patience regarding permission for al-Khadir (peace be upon him) concerning parting from him, in his saying ﴿do not accompany me﴾ [al-Kahf: 76]. What supports this is that in a narration of Muslim: "May Allah's mercy be upon us and upon Musa! Had he not hastened, he would have seen wonders. But he was seized [by a companion's] reproach." He said: "If I ask you about anything after this, do not accompany me." Thus it is established that he fulfilled the standing of the Law which Allah had established for him, and he did not violate the station of patience, which contains nothing contrary to what he knows and recalls of the Law. And how could he not, when he is among the great of the Ulu al-'Azm, of whom Allah the Exalted said, to the most noble of His creation, in encouraging him by their example: ﴿So be patient as the Ulu al-'Azm among the messengers were patient﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35]. And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 90]. And he (peace be upon him) said, as recorded by the two Shaykhs from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was harmed by some of those who were with him at Hunayn, so his face changed color and he said: 'May Allah have mercy on my brother Musa! He was harmed with more than this and was patient.'" It is known that in this story there is much encouragement to boldness in initiating the commanding of good and forbidding of evil, and to perseverance in it, and that one should not defer to anyone, great or small, when a person is confident in his matter outwardly, with the knowledge he has from Allah, His Messenger, and the imams of His religion. And it is a warning that knowledge bestowed directly from Allah (al-'ilm al-ladunni), whether its possessor is a prophet or a saint, does not necessarily entail knowing everything, as some followers of certain Sufis claim, because al-Khadir asked Musa, peace be upon them both: (p-126) "Who are you? Is he Musa, the prophet of the Children of Israel?" as will come. Al-Bukhari related in the Tafsir, through various narrations from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him, related to him, saying: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Musa, the Messenger of Allah, reminded the people one day, until the eyes overflowed and the hearts softened. Then he turned away, and a man caught up with him and said: 'O Messenger of Allah! Is there anyone on earth more knowledgeable than you?' He said: 'No!' So Allah reproached him, because he had not referred the knowledge to Him. He revealed to him: 'Yes! A servant of Mine is at the meeting place of the two seas.' He said: 'My Lord! How can I reach him?' He said: 'Take a fish in a basket, and wherever you lose it, follow it.' In another narration: 'Take a dead fish, and where the spirit is breathed into it.' So he set out, and with him his servant Yusha' ibn Nun, until they reached the rock. Musa placed his head and slept in the shade of the rock, in a moist place. Then the fish stirred—and in another narration: at the root of that rock there was a spring called 'the Life,' and nothing that touched its water failed to come alive. The fish touched the water of that spring, slipped out of the basket, and entered the sea. Allah held back the flow of the sea from it, until its trace was on a stone." His servant said: "I will not wake him." When he awoke, he forgot to tell him. Then he recalled their journey and Musa's saying, peace be upon him: ﴿We have indeed suffered fatigue from this journey of ours﴾ [al-Kahf: 62]. He said: "Allah has already removed the fatigue from you." So they returned and found al-Khadir upon a green cloth on the back of the sea, wrapped in his garment, having placed one end under his feet and the other under his head. Musa greeted him, and he uncovered his face and said: "Is there greeting in my land? Who are you?" He said: "I am Musa." He said: "Musa of the Children of Israel?" He said: "Yes!" He said: "What is your matter?" He said: "I came that you might teach me." He said: "Is it not enough for you that the Torah is in your hands and that revelation comes to you? O Musa! I have a knowledge that it is not fitting for you to know, and you have a knowledge that it is not fitting for me to know," that is, it is not fitting for you to act upon the inner reality, nor for me to stop at the outward; he applied the word "knowledge" to action because it is its cause. So they set off walking along the shore, and they found small ferries carrying the people of this shore to the people of the other shore. Al-Khadir was recognized, and they said: "The righteous servant of Allah! Do not carry him for a wage." So they carried them in their boat without a fare, that is, without payment. They boarded the boat, and a sparrow landed on the edge of the boat and dipped its beak in the sea; in another narration: it took with its beak from the sea; (p-128) and in another narration: it pecked once or twice. He said: "By Allah, my knowledge and your knowledge have not diminished from the knowledge of Allah except as much as this has diminished from the sea." Then suddenly, Musa saw al-Khadir take an axe and split the boat and drive a peg into it. Musa mentioned his objection and the answer, then said: "The first (act) from Musa was forgetfulness, the middle one a condition, and the third deliberate." He related the story, and at its end he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "We wished that Musa had been patient until we were told more about their affair."

Having finished with this story, whose gist is that it concerns travelling through the earth in pursuit of knowledge, he followed it with the story of one who travelled the earth in pursuit of jihad. He placed the first before the second to indicate the high rank of knowledge, since it is the foundation of every happiness and the sustainer of every affair. So He said, linking it to ﴿And those who disbelieve dispute by means of falsehood﴾ [al-Kahf: 56]: ﴿And they ask you about﴾ the righteous, striving man ﴿Dhu'l-Qarnayn﴾ (the Two-Horned). He was so named either for his courage, or because he reached the two horns of the setting and rising of the sun, or because two generations of people passed away in his time, or because he had two braids of hair, or because of his crown [which had two horns]. He is Alexander the First. Ibn Kathir related from al-Azraqi that he lived in the time of Khalil (the Friend, Abraham), peace be upon him, and circumambulated the House with him. Among the formal correspondences (p-129) is that the story of each of the two contains three things, the last of which is the building of a wall without a roof, and that is only for the purpose of protecting what is cared for from the fear of a corrupter. He introduced it with the report of their asking, to indicate that they did not ask about the previous story, despite its wonders, subtleties, secrets and insights, as a rebuke to the Jews for neglecting to ask about it, if their aim was [the truth]; and if it was not their aim, they were all the more deserving of rebuke. Or it may be linked to their first question, which was about the Spirit, and he introduced it with the report of the asking as a reminder of this because of the long separation, to indicate that all of that is connected to their answer as a pearl is connected to its string.

Since it is known that he, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, would say, "How shall I answer them?", He said: ﴿Say﴾, i.e., to them: ﴿I will recite﴾, i.e., I will relate in successive narration in the future time, if Allah informs me of it, ﴿to you﴾, O polytheists and People of the Book who instruct them, qualified by "if Allah wills", as the command concerning it has already passed to you, ﴿a mention of him﴾, sufficient for you in learning his matter, comprehensive of the essentials of his mention.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 84:

Since his story is among the strongest proofs of God's greatness, He presented it in that manifestation and said: ﴿Indeed We﴾, emphasized because the addressees are inclined to obstinacy and denial, ﴿established﴾ him, that is, by the greatness We possess. It was said: by kingship alone; and it was said: together with (p-130) prophethood, because what is attributed to God Most High by way of bounty and kindness is worthy of being understood in its utmost degree, especially when it is expressed through the manifestation of greatness. ﴿He had in the land﴾ a firm establishment (makanah) by which he reached all its routes and by which he prevailed over all its kings. ﴿And We gave him﴾ by Our greatness ﴿of every thing﴾ that he needed for that ﴿a means (sabab)﴾. Abu Hayyan said: The original meaning of sabab is a rope, then it was extended until it came to be applied to whatever is used to reach a goal. So he intended to reach the west, and perhaps he began with it because the gate of repentance is there.

Verse 85 of Surah al-Kahf: ﴿فَأتْبَعَ﴾ means "he followed up" (with the utmost of his effort). This is according to the reading of Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr with the doubled letter (tashdid), and the meaning according to the reading of the rest [of the readers], with the hamza cut and the fa' (taa') left sukun: he joined some means to others, and that is an explanation of the reading with tashdid, "sababan" (a means) by which he would reach it, and he continued following it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 86:

﴿Until, when he reached﴾ in that journey ﴿the setting place of the sun﴾, meaning the limit beyond which no human can go in the west, ("he found it") as far as his sense of touch perceives, ("setting") just as he perceived it with his sense of sight, in that it was connected to what he had reached with his hand, with no barrier between him and it, ﴿in a spring of murky water﴾, meaning one containing hama'ah (black mud), and yet it was hot, just as one who is in the middle of the sea sees that it sets in it and rises from it, while he is certain that the matter is not so. ﴿And he found near it﴾, meaning on the shore adjoining that spring, ("a people") who were disbelievers, having strength over what they attempted and protection. (p-131) So it is as if it were said: what was he commanded regarding them? He was answered with His saying: ("We said") with the manifestation of greatness: ﴿O Dhu'l-Qarnayn﴾, informing him of his nearness to Allah and that he does not act except as He commands him, either through an angel if he was a prophet, which is the most apparent of the possibilities, or through the prophet of his time, or through his own ijtihad (independent reasoning) in his sharia, the correct ijtihad.

﴿Either you punish﴾, meaning these people, by putting the sword among them for their disbelief, ﴿or you adopt﴾, meaning with the utmost of your effort, ﴿regarding them, goodness﴾, a matter of great goodness, and that is beginning with invitation (to faith), indicating that killing, although permissible, is better not to be done except after despair of their returning from what necessitates it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 87:

﴿He said: As for him who does wrong﴾ by persisting in disbelief, We shall be gentle with him until he despairs of it [then -] We shall kill him. To this He alluded with His words: ﴿We shall punish him﴾ with a promise that admits no failure, after a long period of calling him and showing him gentleness, ﴿then he will be returned﴾ after life by death, or after the barzakh (the intermediate state) by resurrection, a return that is at the utmost ease, ﴿to his Lord﴾ who alone has nurtured him, ﴿and He will punish him with a dreadful punishment﴾, severe in the extreme, the like of which he has never known, because of his disbelief in His blessing and his spending of His bounty in worshipping other than Him. In this there is a sign of severe warning to the Jews who deceived the Quraysh, and guidance to the Quraysh to ask them about this statement of theirs, so that it might lead them [to -] acknowledge the resurrection.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 88:

﴿As for him who believes and does righteous deeds﴾, in confirmation of what He has informed of His own confirmation (p-132), ﴿for him there will be﴾ in both abodes ﴿a reward﴾, namely his way being ﴿the best﴾ from Us and from Allah, with [something] better than [it]. ﴿And We will say﴾, by a promise that admits no breaking, after testing him through righteous deeds, ﴿to him﴾, i.e. for his sake, ﴿from Our command﴾, which We command in it, ﴿ease﴾, i.e. a word not burdensome, of prayer, zakat, kharaj, jihad and others, which is what he is able to bear and which does not cause him great hardship.

Then he followed a course (﴿sababan﴾, "a means/path") for his purpose of reaching the rising-place of the sun, from the direction of the south, which would bring him to the east, and he persevered in it without tiring, and no nation he passed by could overcome him.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 90:

﴿Until, when he reached﴾ in that journey of his, ﴿the rising-place of the sun﴾, that is, the place where it first rises upon the inhabited part of the earth, ﴿he found it rising over a people﴾ on the shore of the sea, who had great strength, ﴿for whom We had not made﴾ [and since the intended meaning is generality, he affirmed the prepositional phrase, saying -]: ﴿any shelter against it﴾, that is, from the nearest places to them where it first rises, ”a screen“ that would stand between them and the place from which its rising [is seen -] [from the sea -], whether a mountain, buildings, trees, or anything else.

Since his matter was strange in itself and in being known to others, especially when it was near, Exalted is He said: ﴿Thus﴾, that is, his matter is as we have mentioned to you, in brief summary (p-133) ﴿And We have encompassed﴾ by what We possess of greatness,

﴿what is with him﴾, that is, all of it, from the matters which are the most strange of the strange, ﴿in knowledge﴾, that is, in respect of the inner dimensions of his affairs, let alone their outward aspects. Therefore our informing about that is not to be thought strange, nor is our informing about the matter of the People of the Cave. Nor should it be supposed that the detail of the matter of the Spirit is hidden from Us, for We have knowledge of the hidden aspects of affairs and their outward ones, their witnessed and their unseen. How could it be otherwise, when We Ourselves brought them into existence? But We mention from that only what wisdom calls for. Had We willed, We would have expanded this narrative and the narrative of the People of the Cave, and detailed the matter of the Spirit in a detail that the intelligent would be unable to retain.
Then he followed a means (sababan), in his course toward the region of the barrier, the exit of Ya'juj and Ma'juj, from the direction of the north, and he persisted in that course.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 93:

﴿Until, when he reached﴾ in that journey of his ﴿between the two barriers﴾, that is, the two mountains that prevented those behind them from reaching those in front of them, and they were at the extremity of the land of the Turks on the side adjoining the lands of Armenia and Azerbaijan, both smooth, so that everything slides off them. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read (the sin) with a fatha (al-sin), while the rest read both with a damma. It was said: both mean the same thing. It was also said: the damma-ed form is from the action of God, and the fatha-ed form is from the action of people.

﴿found beside them﴾, that is, near them, on the side that was closer to them, toward the direction from which Dhu al-Qarnayn had come, ﴿a people﴾ (p-134), that is, strong ones, whose language was extremely distant from the languages of the rest of mankind, because their lands were far from the rest of the lands. Therefore, for this reason, ﴿they could scarcely understand speech﴾, that is, they were not close to understanding it well from those who were with Dhu al-Qarnayn, as others understand it. Their description by what follows indicates that they understood only with great difficulty and after long effort, because there was no skilled speaker of their language among those with Dhu al-Qarnayn, and no skilled speaker among them of the language of anyone who was with him. This indicates that between them and the rest of the inhabitants of the earth, other than Ya'juj and Ma'juj, there were vast wastelands and wide deserts that prevented their mingling with them, and that their learning the language of others is very remote, due to the scarcity of their retention, because their lands lie beyond the bounds of moderation, or for some other reason. It follows from this that they could scarcely make others understand any of their speech. This is the meaning of the reading of Hamza and al-Kisa'i with a damma on the first letter (the yaa' of the verb, i.e., yufqihuna) and a kasra on the qaf. It also indicates that their failure to understand and to be understood is restricted to what has passed, [and] His saying:

They said: that is, their translators or their neighbours, those beyond them, as in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud (*Muṣḥaf*, the written copy of the Qur'an), of those who understood some of their speech, or by gesture, as one is addressed to you: ﴿O Dhul-Qarnayn! Indeed Gog and Magog﴾ ﴿have wronged us﴾ (p-135). They are two tribes of mankind from the offspring of Yafith, whose affairs cannot be withstood and whose blaze cannot be extinguished. It is established in the authentic (ṣaḥīḥ) report concerning the resurrection of the Fire that they are from the descendants of Adam, peace be upon him. ﴿They are corrupters in the earth﴾ through every kind of corruption. ﴿So shall we pay you a kharj (a payment, tribute)﴾, which we would bring you from our wealth. This is according to the recitation of the majority (*qirāʾat al-jamāʿa*, the standard reading). Ḥamza and al-Kisā'ī added an alif, so it is read *kharāj*. It has been said that the two have the same meaning. It has also been said that *kharj* is what one gives voluntarily, while *kharāj* (with the alif) is what is obligatory upon you.

﴿On condition that you build﴾ in all of that which is ﴿between us and them﴾ of the land by which they can reach us, with what Allah has given you of power, a *sadd* (barrier, dam) that joins between these two mountains.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 95:

﴿Said﴾ with chastity, piety, and intent toward goodness: ﴿"What my Lord has established me in is better"﴾

Since his establishment (makanah) has two states: the first is outward, namely what is witnessed of his action after it occurs; and the second is inward, which no one reaches by conjecture or supposition, because its like has not been experienced, so the one who discerns by insight (al-mutawassim) does not attain it. Ibn Kathir recited the nun in "makkananee" with clear pronunciation (izhar), while the others recited it with assimilation (idgham), as an indication of both. Since regard is more directed to that in which the establishment [occurs], he put forward his pronoun and said: ﴿"In it my Lord"﴾, that is, the One who has bestowed favor upon me with what you see of wealth and men, and understanding in perfecting affairs, and reaching every possibility attainable for a created being, is ﴿"better"﴾, that is, better than the tribute you intend to give for my establishment, just as Sulayman, upon him be peace, said: "What Allah has given me is better than what He has given you." ﴿"So help me with strength"﴾, that is, with tools and workers by which I may strengthen myself in doing that, for the people of the lands know best what suits this work in their lands, and what I have is only for fighting and its requirements, not for the like of this. ﴿"I will make between you"﴾, that is, between what you are particular to ﴿"and between them a barrier (radman)"﴾, that is, a strong, well-secured barrier, some of it upon the other, with close, tightly joined adherence which necessitates that no part of it be distinguished from another; and it is greater than a dam (sadd). Al-Baghawi said: so he dug the foundation until it reached water, and made its filling of rock and its mortar molten copper poured over it, so that it became like a vein of a mountain beneath the earth.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 18, verse 96:

﴿Ātūnī﴾ with the hamza opened and lengthened, according to the reading of the majority [meaning: give me], and with a connecting hamza (hamzat al-waṣl) followed by a quiescent hamza, meaning: come to me and approach me, for I have answered your request. Then he began, urging them on according to this reading, saying: ﴿zubar al-ḥadīd﴾, meaning: upon it, so bring me a piece. They brought it (p-137), and he piled up what was above the foundation, placing one layer upon another: a layer of iron and a layer of wood. Al-Baghawi said: He kept placing pieces of iron upon the wood and wood upon the iron.

﴿Until, when he had leveled﴾, meaning: with that structure, ﴿between the two cliffs﴾, meaning: the top of the gap between the two mountains described. They were called ṣadafayn (the two facing ones) because they face each other, meaning: they oppose each other and are close together. The reading of those who pronounce the ṣād and the dāl with fatḥah (Nāfiʿ, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, and Ḥafṣ on the authority of ʿĀṣim) [indicates] that their opposition is in the utmost straightness, as though they were a wall in which a door had been opened. The reading of Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, and Ibn ʿĀmir with ḍammah on both indicates that, despite this, it is in the utmost strength, such that its top and bottom are equal. The reading of Shuʿbah on the authority of ʿĀṣim, with ḍammah and the dāl sukūn, indicates the greatest firmness and perfection in each of them, so that neither of them is eroded over a long time by wind or any other decay on one of the two sides through softness from a ... or otherwise. ﴿He said﴾, meaning: to the craftsmen, ﴿Blow﴾ into the bellows, so they blew, and he set fire to it, and this continued ﴿until, when he had made it﴾ (p-138), meaning: all of it, ﴿fire, he said﴾ to the people: ﴿Bring me﴾ copper, ﴿that I may pour over it﴾, meaning: over the heated iron, ﴿molten copper﴾, meaning: copper after it has been melted, for qiṭr is molten copper. This is the reading of Ḥamzah and Abū Bakr on the authority of ʿĀṣim, with the hamza quiescent. The reading of the rest is with fatḥah on the hamza and lengthened, meaning: give me the copper.

So they did that, and it mixed and stuck together, one part to another, and became a solid, hard mountain.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿So they were not able to scale it, nor were they able to pierce it.﴾ That is, as a consequence of this, when he had completed and perfected his work, Ya'juj and Ma'juj and others were unable to ﴿scale it﴾, that is, to climb over its top, because of its height and smoothness, ﴿nor were they able to pierce it﴾ because of its thickness and hardness. The addition of the letter *ta'* here (in *istaṭā'ū*, "were able") indicates that climbing over it is harder than piercing it, because of its height, its hardness, and the joining of its parts to one another until it became a single ingot of iron and copper atop the mountain. Ibn Khurradadhbih has related from Salam al-Turjuman, whom Amir al-Mu'minin al-Wathiq (the Caliph) sent to it, until he saw it, that its height was as far as the eye can reach.
